parts.working: B1 reduces the effect of reaction time / percentage uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest where a fixed reference mark (fiducial marker) should be placed, and why.
parts.answer: At the centre (lowest point) of the swing, because the bob moves fastest there, so the moment it passes can be judged most precisely.
parts.working: B1 at the centre / lowest point of the swing B1 bob moves fastest there – easier to judge when it passes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the temperature of water in a beaker heated on a Bunsen burner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The thermometer is marked in 1 °C intervals. A student records the temperature as 24.37 °C. Comment on this reading.
parts.answer: It is too precise: the thermometer can only be read to about 0.5 °C, so it should be recorded as 24.5 °C (or 24 °C).
parts.working: B1 not possible to read to 0.01 °C – record to nearest 0.5 °C (or 1 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two things the student should do to make sure each temperature reading of the water is accurate.
parts.answer: Stir the water before reading; read the scale with the eye level with the top of the liquid thread (avoid parallax); wait until the reading is steady; keep the bulb fully in the water but not touching the beaker.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: stir; eye level / avoid parallax; wait for reading to stop changing; bulb fully immersed, not touching beaker.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the bulb of the thermometer should not touch the bottom of the beaker when water is being heated from below.
parts.answer: The base of the beaker is hotter than the water, so the reading would be too high.
parts.working: B1 base hotter than the water – reading too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem: You find the density of a small stone collected from the bank of the River Swat. The mass of the stone is 49.6 g. You put water in a measuring cylinder to the 50.0 cm³ mark; after the stone is lowered in, the level is at 68.5 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the stone.
parts.answer: 18.5 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the density of the stone. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.68 g/cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two precautions you should take to obtain an accurate volume.
parts.answer: Lower the stone gently (tilted cylinder / on a thread) so no water splashes out; read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level; make sure no air bubbles cling to the stone; make sure the stone is fully covered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no splashing; eye level with bottom of meniscus; no air bubbles; stone fully submerged; cylinder on a level surface.

author: HomiLabs

stem: You measure the resistance of a resistor using a battery, a switch, an ammeter and a voltmeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the ammeter and voltmeter must be connected in the circuit.
parts.answer: Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel with (across) the resistor.
parts.working: B1 ammeter in series B1 voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before the switch is closed, the ammeter reads 0.02 A. With the switch closed it reads 0.36 A. State the correct current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The voltmeter reads 2.7 V. Calculate the resistance, giving your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the switch should be opened between readings.
parts.answer: To stop the resistor heating up, which would change its resistance.
parts.working: B1 prevents heating / temperature rise changing resistance (and saves the battery).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the thickness of a stack of 200 sheets of exam paper with a ruler at three different places. The readings are 2.18 cm, 2.22 cm and 2.20 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average thickness of the stack in cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of one sheet in mm. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the stack was measured in three places.
parts.answer: The stack may not be the same thickness everywhere (pages not pressed flat), so averaging gives a more representative value.
parts.working: B1 thickness varies / averaging reduces random error.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student used a ruler whose end was slightly worn, so it was measured from the 1.0 cm mark. Explain why this is a sensible technique.
parts.answer: It avoids a zero error caused by the worn end; the reading is taken as the difference between two marks.
parts.working: B1 avoids zero error from worn end.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why calipers would give a better result than a ruler.
parts.answer: Calipers read to 0.1 mm (or better), so the percentage uncertainty in the stack thickness is smaller; they also squeeze the stack evenly.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student traces a ray through a rectangular glass block using optical pins. She draws round the block, marks the normal, and uses two pins on each side of the block.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two techniques that make the positions of the pins and the drawn rays as accurate as possible.
parts.answer: Place the pins well apart (at least 5 cm); look at the bases of the pins when lining them up; draw thin pencil lines; mark pin positions with small crosses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: pins far apart; view bases of pins; thin sharp pencil lines; pins vertical.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The angle of incidence is 40° and the measured angle of refraction is 25°. Calculate the refractive index of the block, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of inaccuracy in measuring the angle of refraction and how it could be reduced.
parts.answer: The normal may not be drawn exactly at 90° to the surface; use a protractor or set square to draw it carefully (or: the block outline may move – draw round it and check its position).
parts.working: B1 source (normal not at 90° / block moved / thick lines / protractor reading) B1 matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
You measure the outside diameter of a test tube in two ways.
Method 1: two set squares are placed against the tube on a ruler. Readings at the edges: 4.3 cm and 5.9 cm. Two more diameters, measured at other points along the tube, are 1.7 cm and 1.6 cm.
Method 2: a thin string is wound 5 times around the tube; the unwound length is 25.6 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the diameter from the first set-square reading and the average diameter from the three readings.
parts.answer: 1.6 cm; average 1.63 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the string measurement to calculate the diameter of the test tube. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: C1 circumference = 25.6 ÷ 5 = 5.12 cm; d = 5.12 ÷ π A1 = 1.63 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the two methods agree within the limits of experimental accuracy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes: 1.63 cm and 1.63 cm differ by much less than 5% (less than 0.1 cm).
parts.working: B1 yes, with difference compared to a stated limit (e.g. within 5% / 0.1 cm).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the set squares should be used to avoid parallax error.
parts.answer: Place the set squares with their vertical edges touching the sides of the tube and resting on the ruler, so the reading is taken straight where the edge meets the scale, viewed from directly above.
parts.working: B1 set square edges perpendicular to ruler, touching tube; read with eye directly above the edge.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the thickness of insulation around a beaker affects the rate of cooling of hot water. You are provided with: beakers, a supply of hot water, cotton wool, a thermometer, a stopwatch, a measuring cylinder. You may also use other apparatus usually found in a school laboratory.
In your plan, you should:
• explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table, or tables, with column headings, to show how you would display your readings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Wrap beakers in different thicknesses of cotton wool (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 cm), add the same volume of hot water at the same starting temperature, record the temperature drop over a fixed time (e.g. 10 min); keep volume, start temperature, beaker size, room temperature, lid same; table: thickness / cm | initial θ / °C | final θ / °C | drop / °C; plot temperature drop against thickness.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: measure thickness with a ruler / use number of layers (B1); same volume of water measured with measuring cylinder (B1 method detail); measure θ at start and after a fixed time, e.g. 10 min (B1); repeat for at least 5 thicknesses (B1); two control variables, e.g. starting temperature, volume of water, size of beaker, room temperature, lid/no lid (B1); table with thickness / cm and temperatures / °C with units (B1); conclusion: plot temperature fall (or rate) against thickness and see whether fall decreases as thickness increases (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the resistance of a metal wire depends on its length. You are provided with: a length of thin constantan wire on a metre rule, a battery, an ammeter, a voltmeter, connecting leads with crocodile clips and a switch.
In your plan, you should:
• describe the circuit (in words) and how you would carry out the investigation
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table with column headings to show how you would display your readings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Connect the battery, switch, ammeter and the wire in series, with the voltmeter across the wire between the crocodile clips. Vary length (e.g. 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 cm), record V and I, calculate R = V/I; keep wire material/diameter and temperature constant (switch off between readings); table l / cm | V / V | I / A | R / Ω; plot R against l – straight line through origin shows R ∝ l.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: correct circuit in words (ammeter in series, voltmeter across the measured length) (B1); measure length between clips with metre rule (B1); record V and I and calculate R = V/I (B1); at least five lengths over a wide range (B1); control: same wire (material, thickness) and constant temperature / switch off between readings / low current (B1); table with l / cm, V / V, I / A, R / Ω (B1); plot R against l; straight line through origin ⇒ proportional (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the angle of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car rolling down it. You are provided with: a long wooden ramp, a toy car, a stack of books, a protractor, a metre rule and a stopwatch.
In your plan, you should:
• explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table with column headings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Set the ramp at angles (e.g. 5°, 10°, 15°, 20°, 25°) measured with a protractor; release the car from rest from the same start line; time it over a fixed measured distance (e.g. 1.00 m), repeat 3 times and average; average speed = distance ÷ time; keep car, distance, release method, ramp surface same; table angle / ° | t₁ / s | t₂ / s | t₃ / s | average t / s | speed / m/s; plot speed against angle.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: measure angle with protractor (or height with rule) (B1); release from rest from same mark – do not push (B1); time over a fixed measured distance (B1); repeat timings and average (B1); at least five angles over a suitable range (B1); control variable, e.g. same car / distance / surface (B1); table with units and conclusion by plotting average speed against angle and describing the trend (B1).

stem: Two methods are used to find the spring constant of the same spring. From a load–extension graph, k = 25.0 N/m. From timing vertical oscillations of a mass on the spring (5 oscillations timed once), k = 23.5 N/m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the two values, using the graph value as the reference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says the two values are equal within the limits of experimental accuracy. State whether you agree, using a 10% limit.
parts.answer: Agree: 6% is within 10%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the method that would make the oscillation value more reliable.
parts.answer: Time more oscillations (e.g. 20) and repeat each timing then average; use a fiducial marker at the centre of oscillation; use smaller amplitude oscillations so the spring stays vertical.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible improvements: more oscillations; repeat and average; fiducial marker; small vertical oscillations.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the load–extension method might give an inaccurate value.
parts.answer: Parallax when reading the ruler beside the spring (eye not level with the pointer), or the ruler not vertical.
parts.working: B1 parallax / ruler not vertical / spring overstretched beyond limit of proportionality.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate whether the colour of a surface affects the rate at which it absorbs infrared radiation. You are provided with: identical metal cans (some painted matt black, matt white, shiny silver), an infrared lamp, thermometers, a stopwatch, a measuring cylinder and water at room temperature.
In your plan, you should:
• explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table with column headings to show how you would display your readings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Put the same volume of water at the same starting temperature in each can, place each the same distance from the infrared lamp (or arrange them at equal distances around it), record temperature every minute for 10 minutes; keep volume, distance, start temperature, lamp power, can size same; table: time / min | θ black / °C | θ white / °C | θ silver / °C; compare temperature rise (or plot θ against t for each) – greatest rise means best absorber.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: same volume of water measured in a measuring cylinder (B1); cans the same distance from the lamp (B1); record temperature at regular intervals or after fixed time (B1); stir before reading / lids with thermometer through hole (B1 technique); two control variables, e.g. initial temperature, lamp power, can size, room conditions (B1); table with time / min and temperatures / °C for each colour (B1); conclusion: compare temperature rises / plot graphs; the largest rise in the same time shows the best absorber (B1).

stem: A student times 10 oscillations of a pendulum with a 50 g bob and then with a 100 g bob, keeping the string length the same. Times: 50 g bob 15.8 s; 100 g bob 16.1 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period for each bob.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student suggests that the period does not depend on the mass of the bob. State whether these results support this, if the experiment is accurate to within 5%. Justify your answer with a calculation.
parts.answer: Yes: the difference is 1.9% of 1.58 s, which is less than 5%.
parts.working: B1 percentage difference ≈ 1.9% (or 0.03 s) B1 within 5% so supports the suggestion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements that would make this conclusion more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more masses (at least five) over a wide range; repeat each timing and average; time 20 oscillations; keep the length (to the centre of the bob) and amplitude exactly the same.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: more masses; repeat and average; more oscillations; keep length measured to centre of bob the same; small, equal amplitude.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the length must be measured to the centre of each bob.
parts.answer: Bobs of different sizes would otherwise give different effective lengths, which changes the period.
parts.working: B1 effective length changes with bob size.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the number of turns of wire on an electromagnet affects its strength. You are provided with: a soft-iron nail, a reel of insulated copper wire, a battery, a variable resistor, an ammeter, a switch and a box of small steel paper clips.
In your plan, you should:
• explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation, including how you would measure the strength
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table with column headings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Wind 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 turns on the nail; connect in series with battery, switch, ammeter and variable resistor; adjust the variable resistor so the current is the same each time; dip the nail end into the clips and count how many are lifted; repeat three times and average; switch off between readings; keep current, nail, clip size the same; table number of turns | clips lifted (1, 2, 3, average); plot average number of clips against number of turns.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: circuit in series with ammeter and variable resistor (B1); strength measured by number of paper clips lifted (B1); adjust variable resistor to keep current constant (key control) (B1); second control, e.g. same nail / same size clips / same part of nail dipped (B1); at least five different numbers of turns, repeated and averaged (B1); table: turns | clips lifted with average (B1); conclusion: plot clips against turns and describe the trend (B1). Safety/precaution: switch off between readings so the wire does not overheat.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the height from which a tennis ball is dropped affects the height of its first bounce. You are provided with: a tennis ball, two metre rules, a clamp stand and a smartphone that can record slow-motion video.
In your plan, you should:
• explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation, including how you would measure the bounce height accurately
• state the key variables to keep constant
• draw a table with column headings
• explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Clamp two metre rules vertically; drop the ball from rest (not thrown) from heights 40–200 cm measured to the bottom of the ball; film the bounce in slow motion against the rule and read the top of the bounce; repeat 3 times and average; keep the same ball, same floor surface, same release method, same measuring point on the ball; table drop height / cm | bounce height 1, 2, 3 / cm | average / cm; plot bounce height against drop height and describe the relationship (e.g. proportional if straight line through origin).
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 7: release from rest from measured height (bottom of ball, eye level / set square) (B1); bounce height measured using slow-motion video against the rule (B1); repeat and average (B1); at least five heights over a wide range (B1); two control variables: same ball, same surface, same temperature/pressure of ball, same reference point (B1); table with heights / cm and average (B1); conclusion: plot bounce height against drop height and state the trend / check for a straight line through the origin (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three identical lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. The current from the battery is 1.5 A. What is the current in each lamp and the potential difference across each lamp?
A 0.50 A and 4.0 V
B 0.50 A and 12 V
C 1.5 A and 4.0 V
D 1.5 A and 12 V
parts.answer: B 0.50 A and 12 V
parts.working: In parallel, each branch has the full 12 V across it, and the supply current divides equally between identical branches: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.50 A. A wrongly shares the p.d. as in a series circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two lamps are connected in parallel across a battery of negligible internal resistance. A third identical lamp is then connected in parallel with them. What happens to the current from the battery and to the brightness of the first lamp?
A current increases; first lamp stays the same brightness
B current increases; first lamp becomes dimmer
C current stays the same; first lamp becomes dimmer
D current decreases; first lamp becomes brighter
parts.answer: A current increases; first lamp stays the same brightness
parts.working: Adding a parallel branch lowers the combined resistance, so the battery current rises. The p.d. across the first lamp is still the battery p.d., so its current and brightness do not change. B would be true for lamps added in series.

stem: A string of 40 identical small lamps used to decorate a house for Eid is connected in series to the 230 V mains supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across each lamp when all the lamps are lit.
parts.working: p.d. shared equally in series (C1): 230 ÷ 40 = 5.75 V (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The current in the string is 0.15 A. Calculate the resistance of one lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The filament of one lamp breaks. State and explain what happens to the other lamps.
parts.answer: They all go out.
parts.working: All lamps go out (B1); the series circuit is broken so there is no current anywhere in it (B1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage of connecting the lamps in a house in parallel rather than in series.
parts.answer: Each lamp can be switched on and off independently / one failing does not affect the others / each gets full mains p.d.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dashboard lamp in a car has a constant resistance of 6.0 Ω. It is connected in series with a variable resistor (rheostat) and a 12 V battery. The rheostat can be set to any value from 0 to 18 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest possible current in the lamp.
parts.working: Largest current when rheostat set to 0 Ω (C1): I = 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 A (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest possible current in the lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across the lamp when the current is smallest.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why increasing the resistance of the rheostat makes the lamp dimmer.
parts.answer: Total resistance rises so current falls; less power in the lamp.
parts.working: Larger total resistance so smaller current (B1); smaller p.d. across / power in lamp so it is dimmer (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student tests two resistors, X and Y, using a 3.0 V supply, an ammeter and a voltmeter. She records:
X alone: p.d. 3.0 V, current 0.20 A
Y alone: p.d. 3.0 V, current 0.30 A
X and Y in series: p.d. 3.0 V, current 0.12 A
X and Y in parallel: p.d. 3.0 V, current 0.50 A

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of each of the four arrangements.
parts.answer: X: 15 Ω; Y: 10 Ω; series: 25 Ω; parallel: 6.0 Ω

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the results for the series and parallel arrangements agree with the rules for combining resistors.
parts.working: Series: R = R₁ + R₂ = 25 Ω (B1); parallel: 1/R = 1/15 + 1/10 gives 6.0 Ω (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the ammeter and the voltmeter were connected.
parts.answer: Ammeter in series with the resistors; voltmeter in parallel across the resistor arrangement.
parts.working: Ammeter in series (B1); voltmeter in parallel with the arrangement being tested (B1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student switched off the supply between readings.
parts.answer: To stop the resistors heating up, which would change their resistance.
parts.working: Prevents heating / keeps temperature (and so resistance) constant (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A battery, a switch, a lamp and a fixed resistor are connected in series. Ammeter A1 is connected between the battery and the switch. Ammeter A2 is connected between the lamp and the resistor. Assume the battery, ammeters and switch have negligible resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammeter A1 reads 0.40 A. State the reading on ammeter A2.
parts.working: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a voltmeter must be connected to measure the potential difference across the lamp.
parts.answer: In parallel with (across) the lamp

parts.label: c
parts.text: The battery has an e.m.f. of 6.0 V and the voltmeter reads 3.5 V across the lamp. Calculate the p.d. across the resistor.
parts.working: Sum of p.d.s in series = e.m.f. (C1): 6.0 − 3.5 = 2.5 V (A1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the resistor.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two resistors of 6.0 kΩ and 3.0 kΩ are connected in series across a 12 V supply to form a potential divider. The output is taken across the 3.0 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A device of resistance 3.0 kΩ is connected across the output. Calculate the combined resistance of the device and the 3.0 kΩ resistor.
parts.answer: 1.5 kΩ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the new output potential difference.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the current from the supply before and after the device is connected.
parts.answer: 1.3 mA before (1.33 mA); 1.6 mA after

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three identical lamps A, B and C each have a resistance of 12 Ω (assume constant). Lamps B and C are connected in parallel with each other, and this pair is connected in series with lamp A across a 9.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combined resistance of the circuit.
parts.working: B and C in parallel: 6.0 Ω (C1); total 12 + 6.0 = 18 Ω (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in lamp A and in lamp B.
parts.working: I = 9.0 ÷ 18 = 0.50 A in A (B1); splits equally, 0.25 A in B (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power of lamp A and of lamp B.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The filament of lamp C breaks. Determine what happens to the brightness of lamp A and of lamp B. Support your answer with a calculation.
parts.answer: A becomes dimmer, B becomes brighter (current 0.375 A in both, about 1.7 W each)
parts.working: New I = 9.0 ÷ 24 = 0.375 A (C1); A dimmer (3.0 W → 1.7 W) and B brighter (0.75 W → 1.7 W) (A1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bar magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive meter, and an e.m.f. is induced. Which change would NOT increase the size of the induced e.m.f.?
A moving the magnet faster
B using a stronger magnet
C using a coil with more turns
D holding the magnet still and moving the coil onto it at the same speed
parts.answer: D holding the magnet still and moving the coil onto it at the same speed
parts.working: The e.m.f. depends on the rate at which field lines are cut; moving the coil instead of the magnet at the same speed gives the same relative motion and the same e.m.f. A, B and C all increase the rate of change of field through the turns.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A transformer has 240 turns on its primary coil and 4800 turns on its secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 12 V a.c. supply and the primary current is 2.0 A. The transformer is 100% efficient. What are the output p.d. and the secondary current?
A 240 V and 0.10 A
B 240 V and 40 A
C 0.60 V and 40 A
D 0.60 V and 0.10 A
parts.answer: A 240 V and 0.10 A
parts.working: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 12 × 4800/240 = 240 V. Power in = power out: 12 × 2.0 = 240 × Is, so Is = 0.10 A. B forgets that a step-up transformer steps the current down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern of the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current.
parts.answer: Concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes at right angles to the wire.
parts.working: Circles around the wire / concentric (B1); centred on the wire, getting further apart with distance (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect on the field of reversing the current.
parts.answer: The direction of the field reverses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the field of increasing the current.
parts.answer: The field becomes stronger (lines closer together).

parts.label: d
parts.text: The wire is now wound into a long solenoid. Describe the magnetic field inside and outside the solenoid.
parts.answer: Inside: strong and uniform (parallel, equally spaced lines). Outside: like the field of a bar magnet.
parts.working: Inside uniform / parallel lines (B1); outside similar to a bar magnet with poles at the ends (B1)

stem: A bicycle dynamo contains a permanent magnet that is turned by the wheel. The magnet rotates inside a fixed coil of wire, which is connected to the bicycle lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an e.m.f. is induced in the coil when the wheel turns.
parts.answer: The rotating magnet changes the magnetic field through the coil (field lines cut the coil), inducing an e.m.f.
parts.working: Magnetic field through coil changes / lines cut the wire (B1); this induces an e.m.f. (electromagnetic induction) (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways of increasing the e.m.f. produced.
parts.answer: Cycle faster (rotate magnet faster); use a stronger magnet; use more turns on the coil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lamp goes out when the bicycle stops.
parts.answer: The magnet stops turning, so the field through the coil no longer changes and no e.m.f. is induced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the output of the dynamo is alternating.
parts.answer: The direction of the field through the coil reverses every half turn, so the e.m.f. reverses direction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A loudspeaker has a light coil of wire attached to a paper cone. The coil sits in the strong magnetic field of a permanent magnet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the loudspeaker produces sound when an alternating current passes through the coil.
parts.answer: The current-carrying coil in the magnet's field feels a force; the force reverses as the current reverses; the coil and cone vibrate and push the air, producing sound waves.
parts.working: Force on current-carrying coil in magnetic field (B1); a.c. makes force reverse direction repeatedly (B1); cone vibrates, producing compressions and rarefactions in the air (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what determines the frequency of the sound produced.
parts.answer: The frequency of the alternating current

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of increasing the size of the current.
parts.answer: Larger force, larger amplitude of vibration, louder sound

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the rule used to predict the direction of the force on the coil.
parts.answer: Fleming's left-hand rule

author: HomiLabs

stem: A phone charger contains a transformer that steps the 230 V a.c. mains down to 5.0 V a.c. before the current is rectified. The primary coil has 1840 turns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
parts.answer: 40 turns

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a transformer does not work with a steady direct current in the primary.
parts.answer: A steady current gives a constant magnetic field in the core; the field through the secondary does not change, so no e.m.f. is induced.
parts.working: d.c. gives an unchanging field (B1); induction needs a changing field, so no output (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the material used for the core and give one reason for using it.
parts.answer: Soft iron; it is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it links the changing field from the primary to the secondary.
parts.working: Soft iron (B1); easily magnetised/demagnetised / concentrates the field through both coils (B1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: The phone takes a current of 2.0 A at 5.0 V. Calculate the current in the primary coil, assuming the transformer is 100% efficient.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a vacuum tube, a narrow beam of electrons travels horizontally from west to east. A uniform magnetic field directed vertically upwards is applied to the region the beam passes through.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction of the force on the electrons when they enter the field.
parts.answer: Horizontally towards the north
parts.working: Conventional current is from east to west (opposite to electron flow) (C1); Fleming's left-hand rule gives force towards the north (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the beam follows a curved path rather than a straight line at an angle.
parts.answer: The force is always at right angles to the direction of motion, so as the beam changes direction the force direction changes too; the path is an arc of a circle.
parts.working: Force perpendicular to velocity (B1); continuously changes direction of motion, giving a curved (circular) path (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the beam of (i) increasing the strength of the magnetic field, (ii) reversing the field.
parts.answer: (i) more sharply curved / deflected more; (ii) deflected towards the south instead

parts.label: d
parts.text: A beam of positive ions travelling in the same direction passes through the same field. State the direction of the force on the ions.
parts.answer: Towards the south
parts.working: Positive charges moving east are a current to the east, so force is opposite to that on electrons (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A small, strong cylindrical magnet is dropped down a vertical copper pipe 1.0 m long. It takes several seconds to emerge. An unmagnetised steel cylinder of the same size falls through in less than half a second. Copper is not a magnetic material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an e.m.f. is induced in the copper pipe as the magnet falls.
parts.answer: The moving magnet's field changes through each ring of copper (the copper cuts the field lines), inducing an e.m.f.
parts.working: Changing magnetic field through the copper / field lines cut (B1); copper is a conductor so an e.m.f. and currents are induced (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the magnet falls slowly.
parts.answer: The induced currents set up magnetic fields that oppose the change causing them (the motion of the magnet), so there is an upward force on the magnet that balances much of its weight.
parts.working: Induced current produces its own magnetic field (B1); direction opposes the change / motion that produced it (B1); so upward (resistive) force on the magnet, smaller acceleration and lower terminal speed (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second copper pipe has a long slit cut along its whole length. State and explain how the falling time changes.
parts.answer: Shorter: currents cannot circulate around the pipe, so the opposing force is much smaller.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the energy transfers while the magnet falls at constant speed.
parts.answer: Gravitational potential energy of the magnet → electrical energy of the induced currents → internal (thermal) energy of the pipe; kinetic energy stays constant.
parts.working: GPE decreases, kinetic energy constant (B1); transferred via induced currents to thermal energy in the pipe (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which unit is equivalent to the volt?
A coulomb per second
B joule per coulomb
C joule per second
D coulomb per joule
parts.answer: B joule per coulomb
parts.working: p.d. = energy transferred ÷ charge, so 1 V = 1 J/C. A is the ampere and C is the watt.

stem: A room heater connected to the 230 V mains takes a current of 4.6 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the heater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge that passes through the heater in 5.0 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the energy transferred by each coulomb of charge passing through the heater.
parts.working: p.d. 230 V means 230 J per coulomb (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why copper is a good electrical conductor and PVC plastic is an insulator.
parts.answer: Copper has many free (delocalised) electrons that can move through it; in PVC the electrons are held in place and cannot move freely.
parts.working: Copper: free electrons that can move (B1); PVC: no / very few free electrons (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the direction of conventional current compares with the direction in which electrons move in a wire.
parts.answer: Opposite: conventional current flows from + to −; electrons flow from − to +.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two materials, other than copper, that are good electrical conductors and two, other than PVC, that are good insulators.
parts.answer: Conductors e.g. aluminium, silver, graphite; insulators e.g. rubber, glass, dry wood.

stem: A torch uses three 1.5 V cells connected in series. Assume the cells have no internal resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total e.m.f. of the three cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One cell is put in the wrong way round. State the e.m.f. of the combination and explain your answer.
parts.working: Reversed cell opposes one of the others (B1): 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5 = 1.5 V (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: With all cells correctly inserted, state the energy given by the battery to each coulomb of charge.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred by the battery when 120 C of charge flows round the circuit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 25 m length of copper cable with a cross-sectional area of 1.5 mm² has a resistance of 0.29 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of 50 m of the same cable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of 25 m of copper cable with a cross-sectional area of 2.5 mm².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of 50 m of the 2.5 mm² cable.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why an electric cooker is connected with thick cable.
parts.answer: Thick cable has lower resistance, so less heating (less power wasted) for the large current; prevents the cable overheating.
parts.working: Larger area → lower resistance (B1); less thermal energy / no overheating with large current (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student investigates how the resistance R of a thin metal wire depends on its length l. She connects lengths of the wire between two crocodile clips and measures the p.d. V across the wire and the current I in it.
l / m: 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00
V / V: 0.29, 0.56, 0.86, 1.12, 1.45
I / A: 0.30, 0.29, 0.30, 0.29, 0.30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance R of the wire for each length. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between R and l shown by the results.
parts.answer: R is (directly) proportional to l

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the resistance per metre of the wire.
parts.answer: 4.8 Ω/m (accept 4.8–4.9 Ω/m)
parts.working: Use R/l, e.g. 4.83 ÷ 1.00 or gradient of R–l graph (C1); 4.8 Ω/m (A1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student switched off the current between readings.
parts.answer: To stop the wire heating up, which would increase its resistance.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the length l may not be measured accurately.
parts.answer: The crocodile clips have a width, so the exact contact point is uncertain / the wire may not be straight.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A small lamp in a solar garden light has a p.d. of 3.0 V across it and a current of 0.25 A in it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge that flows through the lamp in 10 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred in the lamp in this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by the potential difference across a component.
parts.answer: The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge passing through the component.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the lamp at this p.d.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures the current I in a semiconductor diode for different p.d.s V across it.
V / V: −1.0, 0, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80
I / mA: 0, 0, 0, 0.1, 2.0, 12, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the current in the diode depends on the p.d. across it.
parts.answer: No current for reverse p.d. or small forward p.d.; current starts at about 0.4–0.5 V and then rises very rapidly with p.d.
parts.working: Zero current in reverse (B1); little current until about 0.5 V, then increases steeply (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the diode at 0.60 V and at 0.80 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the diode does not obey Ohm's law.
parts.answer: Its resistance changes with p.d.; current is not proportional to p.d.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one use of a diode.
parts.answer: Rectification (converting a.c. to d.c.) / protecting a circuit from a reversed battery

author: HomiLabs

stem: A wire carries a steady current of 0.80 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge that passes a point in the wire in 1.0 minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the number of electrons passing the point in this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same current passes through a thinner section of the wire. State whether the number of electrons passing a point each second in the thinner section is larger, smaller or the same, and explain.
parts.answer: The same, because the current (charge per second) is the same at all points in series.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A car battery has an e.m.f. of 12 V and is labelled '60 A h' (it can supply a current of 60 A for one hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the battery can deliver about 2.2 × 10⁵ C of charge when fully charged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy the battery can transfer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When the engine is started, the starter motor takes 150 A for 2.5 s. Calculate the percentage of the battery's charge used.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures the current I in a resistor at constant temperature for different p.d.s V.
V / V: 0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0
I / A: 0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between I and V shown by the results, and name the law it illustrates.
parts.answer: I is directly proportional to V; Ohm's law

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the current when the p.d. is 7.5 V.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The resistor is replaced by a filament lamp. Describe how the shape of the I–V graph would differ.
parts.answer: It curves: the gradient decreases as V increases (resistance increases as the filament heats).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A negatively charged rod is held close to, but not touching, an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. Which describes the sphere while the rod is held there?
A the side near the rod becomes positive and the far side becomes negative
B the side near the rod becomes negative and the far side becomes positive
C the whole sphere becomes positively charged
D there is no separation of charge on the sphere
parts.answer: A the side near the rod becomes positive and the far side becomes negative
parts.working: Free electrons in the metal are repelled by the negative rod and move to the far side, leaving the near side positive (charging by induction). The sphere's total charge stays zero, so C is wrong.

stem: Sana rubs a rubber balloon on her dry hair. The balloon becomes negatively charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the balloon becomes negatively charged.
parts.answer: Friction transfers electrons from the hair to the balloon.
parts.working: Electrons move (B1); from hair to balloon (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the charge left on the hair.
parts.answer: Positive

parts.label: c
parts.text: The balloon is placed against a wall and sticks to it. Explain why.
parts.answer: The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface, leaving it positive nearby; opposite charges attract.
parts.working: Charge separation / induced positive charge on wall surface (B1); attraction between opposite charges (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a polythene rod can be charged by rubbing it with a cloth, but a copper rod held in the hand cannot.
parts.answer: In polythene (insulator) electrons cannot move, so the charge stays where it was rubbed. In copper (conductor) electrons move freely, so any charge flows through the rod and the person's body to earth.
parts.working: Insulator: charges cannot move / stay on surface (B1); conductor: free electrons move (B1); charge conducted to earth through the hand (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the copper rod could be given a charge by rubbing.
parts.answer: Hold it by an insulating handle (so the charge cannot escape to earth).

stem: A negatively charged polythene rod hangs horizontally from a nylon thread so that it can turn freely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A second negatively charged polythene rod is brought close to one end of the hanging rod. State and explain what happens.
parts.answer: The hanging rod moves away (is repelled) because like charges repel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A positively charged acetate rod is brought close instead. State and explain what happens.
parts.answer: The hanging rod moves towards it (is attracted) because unlike charges attract.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the unit of electric charge.
parts.answer: coulomb (C)

author: HomiLabs

stem: On a hot, dry day in Karachi, a passenger slides across the plastic seat of a car. When she gets out and touches the metal door, she feels a small electric shock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the passenger becomes charged.
parts.answer: Friction between clothes and the seat transfers electrons, so the passenger gains (or loses) electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the passenger feels a small shock on touching the metal door.
parts.answer: Charge flows suddenly between the passenger and the metal (to earth), and this current through the body is felt as a shock.
parts.working: Metal is a conductor / path for charge (B1); sudden flow of charge (discharge) through the body (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this happens less often on humid days.
parts.answer: Moist air and damp surfaces conduct slightly, so charge leaks away before it builds up.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A lightning stroke during a monsoon storm carries an average current of 25 kA for 0.20 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge transferred by the lightning stroke.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charge on an electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the number of electrons transferred.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The p.d. between the cloud and the ground is 1.0 × 10⁸ V. Calculate the energy transferred by the stroke.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A metal sphere stands on an insulating base. A student has a negatively charged polythene rod.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to give the sphere a positive charge using only the negatively charged rod and an earth connection, without the rod touching the sphere.
parts.answer: Bring the negative rod near the sphere; electrons are repelled to the far side; touch the far side with an earth wire (or finger) so electrons flow to earth; remove the earth connection while the rod is still near; then remove the rod.
parts.working: Rod brought near, electrons repelled (B1); sphere earthed so electrons flow away to earth (B1); earth removed before rod (B1); rod removed, sphere left positive (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the charge is found on the sphere at the end.
parts.answer: Spread over the outer surface of the sphere

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an inkjet printer, tiny drops of ink are given an electric charge and then pass between two horizontal metal plates with a large p.d. between them. The plates steer the drops onto the paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a charged ink drop is deflected as it passes between the plates.
parts.answer: There is an electric field between the plates, which exerts a force on the charged drop towards the oppositely charged plate.
parts.working: Electric field between plates (B1); force on charge (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the deflection changes if a drop carries a larger charge.
parts.answer: Larger deflection (larger force)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The drops are negatively charged and must be deflected upwards. State which plate must be positive.
parts.answer: The upper plate

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why uncharged drops pass straight through.
parts.answer: No charge, so no electric force acts on them.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a car factory in Karachi, paint is sprayed from a nozzle that gives every droplet a positive charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the paint droplets spread out into a fine, even cloud.
parts.answer: All droplets have the same sign of charge, so they repel each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The car body is given the opposite charge. Explain why paint reaches the back and edges of the panel as well as the front.
parts.answer: The droplets are attracted to the oppositely charged car body; the electric field lines curve round to the back surfaces so droplets follow them.
parts.working: Opposite charges attract (B1); attraction acts on all surfaces / droplets wrap round (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two advantages of electrostatic spraying compared with ordinary spraying.
parts.answer: Less paint wasted; more even coat; paint reaches hard-to-reach places.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a flour mill in Faisalabad, fine flour is blown at high speed through long pipes into storage silos.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large static charge can build up on the pipes and the flour.
parts.answer: Friction between the moving flour grains and the pipe walls transfers electrons; if the pipe or flour is insulated, the charge cannot escape and builds up.
parts.working: Friction / rubbing transfers electrons (B1); charge cannot flow away from insulated parts (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: A spark may jump when the charge discharges, which can ignite the fine flour dust and cause an explosion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two precautions the mill can take.
parts.answer: Earth all metal pipes and machinery; use conducting pipes; keep the air humid; bond parts together with conducting straps.

author: HomiLabs

stem: After being rubbed, a balloon has a charge of −4.8 × 10⁻⁸ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of extra electrons on the balloon. The charge on an electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mass of an electron is 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Calculate the increase in mass of the balloon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on whether this change in mass could be detected with a laboratory balance.
parts.answer: No; it is far too small (many orders of magnitude below a balance's resolution).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two horizontal metal plates are placed one above the other. The upper plate is connected to the positive terminal of a high-voltage supply and the lower plate is earthed. A tiny charged oil drop between the plates is held stationary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction of the electric field between the plates.
parts.answer: Vertically downwards (from the positive upper plate to the lower plate)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce whether the oil drop is positively or negatively charged. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Negative
parts.working: Weight acts downwards, so electric force must be upwards (B1); upward force is opposite to the field direction, so the charge is negative (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The drop picks up some extra electrons. Describe its motion now.
parts.answer: It accelerates upwards (towards the positive plate).
parts.working: Electric force now larger than weight (B1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: The supply is switched off. Describe the motion of the drop.
parts.answer: It falls (accelerates downwards under its weight).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An LED television connected to the 230 V mains takes a current of 0.26 A. What is its power?
A 0.26 W
B 60 W
C 230 W
D 885 W
parts.answer: B 60 W
parts.working: P = IV = 0.26 × 230 = 59.8 W ≈ 60 W. D comes from dividing 230 by 0.26, which gives a resistance, not a power.

stem: An electric kettle is rated 2.2 kW, 230 V. It is switched on for 3.0 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred by the kettle in 3.0 minutes, in joules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in the kettle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express the energy in (a) in kilowatt-hours.
parts.answer: 0.11 kW h

author: HomiLabs

stem: A family replaces a 60 W filament lamp with a 9.0 W LED lamp that gives the same light. The lamp is used for 6.0 hours each day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy used in 30 days by each lamp, in kW h.
parts.answer: LED 1.62 kW h; filament lamp 10.8 kW h

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electricity costs Rs 50 per kW h. Calculate the money saved in 30 days by using the LED lamp.
parts.answer: Rs 459

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the LED lamp gives the same light for much less power.
parts.answer: It wastes much less energy as thermal energy (it is more efficient).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 150 Ω resistor in an electric fan heater carries a current of 0.40 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the resistor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy produced in 5.0 minutes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The electricity meter of a house in Lahore reads 24 615 kW h at the start of a month and 25 043 kW h at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of units (kW h) used in the month.
parts.answer: 428 kW h

parts.label: b
parts.text: The first 200 units cost Rs 30 each and every further unit costs Rs 45. Calculate the bill for the month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The month has 30 days. Calculate the average power used by the household, in kW.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric water heater (geyser) has a power of 3.0 kW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The geyser heats 50 kg of water from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C). Calculate the energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortest time the geyser could take to do this, in minutes.
parts.answer: 35 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: It actually takes 40 minutes. Calculate the efficiency of the geyser.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A phone charger supplies 2.0 A at 5.0 V to a phone for 1.5 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the power supplied by the charger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy supplied in 1.5 hours, in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this energy in kW h.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The phone is charged like this every day for a year (365 days) at Rs 50 per kW h. Calculate the yearly cost.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric heater is rated 1000 W when connected to 230 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the heater element.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a summer evening the mains p.d. drops to 200 V. Calculate the power of the heater now, assuming its resistance is unchanged.
parts.answer: 756 W (about 760 W)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the effect of this on the time needed to warm a room.
parts.answer: It takes longer (less energy transferred each second).

author: HomiLabs

stem: During load-shedding, a home in Multan uses a UPS. Its 12 V battery is rated 200 A h. The UPS inverter runs a 75 W ceiling fan and four 12 W LED lamps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total power of the appliances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the fully charged battery, in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The inverter is 85 % efficient. Calculate how long the battery can run the appliances, in hours.
parts.answer: 16.6 h (about 17 h)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the real running time is shorter.
parts.answer: The battery should not be fully discharged / battery capacity falls with age or high current.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric car has a 40 kW h battery. It is charged at home from 20 % to 80 % of full charge using a 7.4 kW charger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy that must be stored in the battery.
parts.answer: 24 kW h

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charging process is 90 % efficient. Calculate the energy taken from the mains.
parts.answer: 26.7 kW h

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the charging time.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Electricity costs Rs 55 per kW h. Calculate the cost of this charge.
parts.answer: Rs 1467 (about Rs 1470)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two filament lamps are labelled '230 V, 60 W' and '230 V, 100 W'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of each lamp when working normally.
parts.answer: 60 W lamp: 882 Ω; 100 W lamp: 529 Ω

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two lamps are connected in series across the 230 V supply. Assuming the resistances do not change, calculate the current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power of each lamp in the series circuit and state which lamp is brighter.
parts.answer: 60 W lamp: 23 W; 100 W lamp: 14 W; the 60 W lamp is brighter
parts.working: P = I²R for each (C1); 23.4 W and 14.1 W (A1); the 60 W lamp (larger resistance) is brighter (A1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 1.2 kW, 230 V clothes iron is used for 40 minutes. A thermostat switches the heater on and off, so that the heater is on for 60 % of the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred in kW h.
parts.answer: 0.48 kW h

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electricity costs Rs 50 per kW h. Calculate the cost.
parts.answer: Rs 24

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current in the iron while the heater is on.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the heating element.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metal is NOT attracted by a magnet?
A iron
B nickel
C cobalt
D copper
parts.answer: D copper
parts.working: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic (ferromagnetic) materials; copper is non-magnetic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to use a small plotting compass to draw the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet placed on a sheet of paper.
parts.answer: Place the compass near the N pole; mark the position of the needle's N end with a dot; move the compass so its tail is at the dot and mark again; repeat to reach the S pole; join the dots and add an arrow; repeat from other starting points.
parts.working: Compass near a pole, mark direction of needle (B1); move compass along, marking successive points (B1); join dots into a line with arrow; repeat for several lines (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the field lines outside the magnet.
parts.answer: From the N pole to the S pole

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the field is strongest and how this is shown by the field lines.
parts.answer: At the poles; the field lines are closest together there.
parts.working: At the poles (B1); lines closest together (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a chain of steel paper clips can hang from the N pole of a magnet.
parts.answer: Each clip becomes magnetised by induction (induced magnetism) and then attracts the next clip.
parts.working: Induced magnetism in each clip (B1); each clip becomes a magnet that attracts the next (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chain of soft iron nails and a chain of steel pins are both pulled off the magnet. State which chain stays together, and explain.
parts.answer: The steel pins: steel keeps its magnetism (permanent), while soft iron loses it almost at once (temporary).
parts.working: Steel pins (B1); steel retains magnetism, iron does not (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether soft iron is used for permanent magnets or temporary magnets.
parts.answer: Temporary magnets (e.g. electromagnet cores)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to magnetise a steel bar using a solenoid.
parts.answer: Place the bar inside a solenoid and pass a direct current through the solenoid, then switch off and remove the bar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways of demagnetising the bar.
parts.answer: Heating it strongly; hammering it; placing it in a solenoid carrying a.c. and slowly pulling it out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test to show the bar has become a magnet.
parts.answer: Bring one end near a known magnet's pole: if it repels, the bar is a magnet.

stem:
A student wraps different numbers of turns of insulated wire around the same iron nail. With a current of 1.5 A each time, she counts how many identical steel paper clips the nail can lift.
number of turns: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
number of clips lifted: 3, 7, 10, 14, 17

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: number of turns; dependent: number of paper clips lifted

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Current; size/material of the iron core; type and size of paper clips; the way the clips are picked up

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the results.
parts.answer: The number of clips increases with the number of turns, roughly in proportion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the number of clips is not a very precise measure of the strength of the electromagnet.
parts.answer: It can only change in whole clips / clips can hang from each other as well as from the core.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Predict the number of clips lifted with 60 turns.
parts.answer: about 20 (accept 20–21)
parts.working: Continuing the pattern: about 0.34 clips per turn × 60 ≈ 20 (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: The north pole of one bar magnet faces the south pole of another, with a gap of 4 cm between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the magnetic field in the gap between the poles.
parts.answer: Uniform: straight, parallel, equally spaced field lines going from the N pole to the S pole.
parts.working: Parallel, equally spaced lines (B1); direction N to S (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A plotting compass is placed in the middle of the gap. State the direction in which its N end points.
parts.answer: Towards the S pole (away from the N pole)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two properties of magnetic field lines.
parts.answer: They never cross; closer lines mean a stronger field; they point from N to S outside a magnet.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When the key of a car is turned, a small current flows through a relay coil. The relay switches on the starter motor, which needs a current of about 150 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the relay allows a small current in the ignition-switch circuit to switch on the large starter-motor current.
parts.answer: A small current in the relay coil magnetises its soft iron core; the electromagnet attracts an iron armature; this closes the contacts in the separate high-current circuit, so the motor runs.
parts.working: Current in coil makes an electromagnet (B1); attracts iron armature / switch (B1); closes contacts in motor circuit (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the starter motor is not switched directly by the ignition switch.
parts.answer: The motor current is very large, needing thick cables; the ignition switch and the wires to it can then be small; the driver is kept away from the high-current circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the material used for the core of the relay coil.
parts.answer: Soft iron

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet.
parts.answer: It can be switched on and off; its strength can be changed by changing the current (or number of turns); it can be made very strong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of a permanent magnet in the home and explain why a permanent magnet is suitable.
parts.answer: e.g. a fridge door seal / cupboard catch; it needs no electricity and the force is always present.
parts.working: Valid use (B1); reason linked to it (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A steel spoon is attracted by both the N and the S pole of a magnet. Explain why it is never repelled.
parts.answer: The spoon is unmagnetised; the pole induces the opposite pole in the near end, so there is always attraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The N end of a compass needle points towards the Earth's geographic North Pole. Deduce what kind of magnetic pole lies near the geographic North Pole. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: A magnetic south pole
parts.working: Unlike poles attract (B1); the N end of the needle is attracted, so it is an S pole (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the Earth's magnetic field.
parts.answer: Similar to the field of a large bar magnet inside the Earth

parts.label: c
parts.text: A compass placed near a steel filing cabinet points in a wrong direction. Explain why.
parts.answer: The steel becomes magnetised (by induction or permanently) and its field adds to the Earth's field, so the needle aligns with the combined field.
parts.working: Steel is magnetic / magnetised (B1); its field changes the field at the compass (B1)

stem: At a recycling centre in Islamabad, a moving belt carries a mixture of steel and aluminium drink cans under a large electromagnet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why unmagnetised steel cans are attracted by the magnet.
parts.answer: The magnet induces magnetism in the steel, with an opposite pole on the near side, so they attract.
parts.working: Induced magnetism (B1); opposite pole induced nearer the magnet, so attraction (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an electromagnet is used rather than a permanent magnet.
parts.answer: It can be switched off to drop the steel cans into a separate bin; its strength can be adjusted.
parts.working: Can be switched off to release cans (B1); second valid point (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the aluminium cans are left behind.
parts.answer: Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so no magnetism is induced in it.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A soft iron bar is placed in line with a strong bar magnet, close to its N pole but not touching.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the magnetic pole induced at the end of the iron bar nearest the magnet, and at its far end.
parts.answer: Near end: S pole; far end: N pole

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second soft iron bar touches the far end of the first. State the pole induced at the end of the second bar touching the first.
parts.answer: S pole

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the second bar is held less strongly than the first.
parts.answer: It is further from the magnet, so the field and induced magnetism are weaker.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The magnet is removed. State and explain what happens to the bars.
parts.answer: They fall apart / lose almost all their magnetism, because soft iron is a temporary magnet.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has two identical-looking steel bars, P and Q. One is a magnet; the other is unmagnetised. No other equipment is available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student can find out which bar is magnetised, using only the two bars.
parts.answer: Hold bar P and touch one end of it on the middle of bar Q, then swap. When the magnet's end touches the middle of the unmagnetised bar there is strong attraction; when the unmagnetised bar's end touches the middle of the magnet there is little or no force, as the magnet's field is weakest at its middle.
parts.working: Touch end of one to middle of the other (B1); then the other way round (B1); strong attraction identifies the bar whose END was used as the magnet (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why attraction alone cannot show that a bar is a magnet, but repulsion can.
parts.answer: A magnet attracts both a magnet and unmagnetised magnetic material; repulsion only happens between two magnets (like poles).
parts.working: Attraction also occurs with unmagnetised iron/steel (B1); repulsion needs two magnets (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the truth table for a two-input NAND gate, giving the output Q for the inputs A, B = 00, 01, 10 and 11.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a NAND gate is related to an AND gate.
parts.answer: Its output is the inverse of the AND output (AND followed by NOT).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of different input combinations for a three-input gate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A logic gate has the truth table: A = 0, B = 0, Q = 1; A = 0, B = 1, Q = 0; A = 1, B = 0, Q = 0; A = 1, B = 1, Q = 0. Name the gate.
parts.answer: NOR gate

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the outputs of an OR gate for the same four input combinations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what logic 1 and logic 0 mean in an electronic circuit.
parts.answer: Logic 1 is a high voltage (close to the supply voltage, 'on'); logic 0 is a low voltage (close to 0 V, 'off').

stem: A shop has a front door and a rear door. Sensor F gives 1 when the front door is open and sensor R gives 1 when the rear door is open. An alarm must sound when either door, or both, is open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the logic gate needed.
parts.answer: OR gate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write out the truth table for the alarm output Q for all inputs F and R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner adds a key switch K that gives 1 when the alarm is set. The alarm must sound only when it is set and a door is open. State the extra gate needed and how it is connected.
parts.answer: An AND gate; its inputs are the OR gate output and K, and its output drives the alarm.
parts.working: AND gate (B1); inputs = OR output and K (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the output of a NOT gate whose input is 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the output of an AND gate with inputs 1 and 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the output of an OR gate with inputs 0 and 0.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the output of a NOR gate with inputs 0 and 1.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State the output of a NAND gate with inputs 0 and 0.

stem: A car has a seat-belt warning buzzer. Sensor I gives 1 when the ignition is on. Sensor S gives 1 when the seat belt is fastened. The buzzer must sound only when the ignition is on and the seat belt is not fastened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a combination of logic gates that sounds the buzzer correctly.
parts.answer: Pass S through a NOT gate; feed the NOT output and I into an AND gate whose output drives the buzzer.
parts.working: NOT gate on S (B1); AND gate with I (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write out the truth table for the buzzer output Q for all inputs I and S.
parts.working: Correct NOT S column (B1); Q = 1 only for I = 1, S = 0 (B2)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A greenhouse sprinkler must switch on only when the soil is dry and it is dark (to reduce evaporation). Sensor D gives 1 when the soil is dry. Sensor L gives 1 in daylight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a combination of logic gates to control the sprinkler.
parts.answer: L goes through a NOT gate; NOT L and D are the inputs of an AND gate.
parts.working: NOT on L (B1); AND with D (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write out the truth table for Q for all inputs D and L.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A manual switch M (1 = on) is added through an OR gate so that the sprinkler also runs whenever M = 1. State how many of the 8 combinations of D, L and M make the sprinkler run.
parts.working: M = 1 gives 4 combinations (C1); plus D = 1, L = 0, M = 0 (A1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Inputs A and B are connected to an OR gate. The output of the OR gate and a third input C are connected to an AND gate, whose output is Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write out the full truth table for Q for all eight combinations of A, B and C.
parts.working: Correct OR column (B1); Q = 1 only when C = 1 and A or B = 1 (B2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many combinations give Q = 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe in words when Q is 1.
parts.answer: When C is 1 and at least one of A and B is 1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a NAND gate can be used as a NOT gate.
parts.answer: Join the two inputs together; then input 0 gives NAND(0,0) = 1 and input 1 gives NAND(1,1) = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two NAND gates can be combined to act as an AND gate.
parts.answer: Feed A and B into the first NAND gate; connect its output to both inputs of a second NAND gate (used as NOT).
parts.working: First NAND with A and B (B1); output inverted by second NAND with inputs joined (B1)

stem: The drum motor of a washing machine must run only when the door is closed (D = 1), the water is at the correct level (W = 1) and the start button has been pressed (S = 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how two two-input AND gates can be connected to give the correct output.
parts.answer: D and W go into the first AND gate; its output and S go into the second AND gate, which drives the motor.
parts.working: First AND for two inputs (B1); its output and the third input into the second AND (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many of the 8 input combinations switch the motor on.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an AND arrangement is a sensible safety design here.
parts.answer: The motor cannot run unless every safety condition is met, e.g. the door is closed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a NOR gate can act as a NOT gate.
parts.answer: Join the inputs: NOR(0,0) = 1 and NOR(1,1) = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two NOR gates can be connected to make an OR gate.
parts.answer: A and B into a NOR gate; its output into both inputs of a second NOR gate (acting as NOT).
parts.working: NOR of A and B (B1); inverted by a second NOR (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how three NOR gates can be connected to make an AND gate. Show that your arrangement works for A = 1, B = 1 and for A = 1, B = 0.
parts.answer: Invert A with one NOR (inputs joined) and B with another; feed NOT A and NOT B into a third NOR. A = 1, B = 1: inputs 0, 0 → output 1. A = 1, B = 0: inputs 0, 1 → output 0.
parts.working: Two NORs as NOT gates on A and B (B1); third NOR combines them (B1); both checks correct (B1)

stem: A logic circuit has output Q = (A OR B) AND NOT(A AND B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write out a truth table for A, B, (A OR B), (A AND B), NOT(A AND B) and Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe in words when Q is 1.
parts.answer: When the inputs are different (exactly one input is 1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A stair light is controlled by switch A at the bottom and switch B at the top using this circuit. Explain why the light can be changed from either switch.
parts.answer: Changing either input alone changes whether the inputs are the same or different, so the output always changes.
parts.working: Changing one input changes Q (B1); true whichever switch is changed / whatever the other switch's state (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Input A goes through one NOT gate and input B through another. The two NOT outputs are the inputs of an AND gate with output Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write out the truth table for this circuit, including columns for NOT A and NOT B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the single gate that has the same truth table.
parts.answer: NOR

parts.label: c
parts.text: The AND gate is replaced by an OR gate. Name the single gate that the new circuit is equivalent to, and give the output for A = 1, B = 1.
parts.answer: NAND; output 0

author: HomiLabs

stem: Inputs A and B go into a NAND gate whose output is P. P and A are then the two inputs of a second NAND gate, whose output is Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write out the truth table showing P and Q for all four combinations of A and B.
parts.working: P column (B1); Q for each row correct (B3; −1 per error)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the only combination of inputs for which Q = 0.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A tailoring workshop in Lahore has several electrical hazards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The plastic insulation on the cable of a sewing machine is cracked, exposing a wire. State the hazard.
parts.answer: Electric shock (and risk of fire from a short circuit)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Six appliances are plugged into one adapter in a single socket. Explain the hazard.
parts.answer: The total current is very large, so the socket and cables overheat; this may cause a fire.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A worker uses a steam iron while her hands are wet. Explain the hazard.
parts.answer: Water conducts and lowers the resistance of the skin, so a larger current could pass through her body if she touched a live part: a serious shock.
parts.working: Water conducts / lowers resistance (B1); larger current through body, shock (B1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three wires in a three-core mains cable and state the colour of the insulation on each.
parts.answer: Live: brown; neutral: blue; earth: green and yellow stripes
parts.working: One mark per wire with correct colour (B1 × 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which wire the fuse is connected to.
parts.answer: Live

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which wire is normally at or close to 0 V.
parts.answer: Neutral (the earth wire is also at 0 V)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens inside a fuse when the current becomes too large.
parts.answer: The thin fuse wire heats up and melts, breaking the circuit.
parts.working: Wire heats (B1); melts and breaks circuit / stops current (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fuse chosen should have a rating just above the normal working current of the appliance.
parts.answer: It must not blow during normal use, but must blow if the current rises much above normal, before cables overheat.
parts.working: Not blow in normal use (B1); blows quickly for a fault current (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what should be done before a blown fuse is replaced.
parts.answer: Switch off/unplug and find and repair the fault.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a circuit breaker (trip switch) does.
parts.answer: It automatically switches off (breaks) the circuit when the current becomes too large.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of a circuit breaker over a fuse.
parts.answer: It can be reset easily; it does not need replacing; it acts faster.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A circuit breaker trips every time an old kettle is switched on. Suggest two possible reasons.
parts.answer: A fault in the kettle (e.g. a short circuit or live touching the case); too many appliances on the same circuit (overload).

stem: A washing machine has a metal case connected to the earth wire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fault causes the live wire to touch the metal case. Explain how the earth wire and the fuse protect the user.
parts.answer: The earth wire gives a low-resistance path from the case to earth; a very large current flows through the live and earth wires; the fuse melts and disconnects the live supply, so the case is no longer live.
