parts.working: Low-resistance path to earth (B1); large current (B1); fuse melts and cuts off the live supply (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the earth wire must have a low resistance.
parts.answer: So that the fault current is large enough to blow the fuse quickly (and the case stays near 0 V).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three appliances work on the 230 V mains: a 1.2 kW microwave oven, a 60 W table lamp and a 1.0 kW iron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal current in each appliance.
parts.answer: Microwave 5.2 A; lamp 0.26 A; iron 4.3 A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. State the fuse that should be fitted in the plug of each appliance.
parts.answer: Microwave 13 A; lamp 3 A; iron 5 A
parts.working: One mark each; smallest rating above the normal current (B1 × 3)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the switch of an appliance must be in the live wire, not the neutral wire.
parts.answer: When the switch is off, the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage of the live wire, so touching its internal parts is safe.
parts.working: With switch in live, appliance not at high potential when off (B1); with switch in neutral, parts would still be live — shock risk (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fuse must also be in the live wire.
parts.answer: When the fuse melts, the appliance is cut off from the live supply, so it is no longer at a dangerous potential.
parts.working: Disconnects the live (high-voltage) side (B1); so no shock from the appliance after the fuse blows (B1)

stem: An extension lead rated at 13 A is used on the 230 V mains to run a 2.0 kW heater, a 2.2 kW kettle and a 1.1 kW iron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total current taken when all three appliances are used together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: The current is much larger than the 13 A rating; the cable and adapter overheat, which may melt the insulation and start a fire (or the fuse blows).
parts.working: Current exceeds rating (B1); overheating / fire risk (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total power that can safely be connected to the extension lead.
parts.answer: 2990 W (about 3.0 kW)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cable to an electric oven is much thicker than the cable to a table lamp.
parts.answer: The oven takes a much larger current; a thick cable has low resistance so less heating, preventing overheating.
parts.working: Large current (B1); thick cable, low resistance, less heating (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cable has a total resistance of 0.10 Ω and carries 30 A. Calculate the power dissipated in the cable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the same cable when the current is 13 A.

stem: A small reading lamp normally takes a current of 0.50 A from the mains. Its plug is fitted with a 13 A fuse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: If a fault makes the current rise to several amps, the 13 A fuse will not melt, so the thin flex can overheat and catch fire.
parts.working: Fuse would not blow for a fault current below 13 A (B1); thin flex overheats / fire (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the fuse that should be fitted.
parts.answer: 3 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why even the correct fuse does not protect a person who touches a live wire.
parts.answer: A current of a few tens of milliamps through the body can kill, which is far too small to melt a fuse.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A metal kettle is earthed and protected by a 13 A fuse on 230 V mains. A fault connects the live wire to the case. The total resistance of the fault path through the live and earth wires is 0.50 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current that flows in the fault.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the 13 A fuse.
parts.answer: It melts (blows) almost instantly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The earth wire has come loose. A person with a body resistance of 2000 Ω touches the live case while standing on a wet floor. Calculate the current through the person.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Comment on the danger in (c).
parts.answer: 115 mA can stop the heart and is far below 13 A, so the fuse does not blow: it may be fatal.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is dangerous if the fuse in an appliance is wrongly placed in the neutral wire.
parts.answer: If a fault makes the fuse blow, the appliance stops working but stays connected to the live wire; its internal parts (or a faulty case) are still at 230 V; anyone touching them could get a shock.
parts.working: Fuse blows, appliance off (B1); but still connected to live (B1); risk of shock even when it seems off (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the appliance still stops working when this fuse blows.
parts.answer: The circuit is broken, so no current flows through the appliance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current through a person's body on the 230 V mains when the body resistance is (i) 100 kΩ (dry skin), (ii) 1.0 kΩ (wet skin).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why mains sockets are not fitted in bathrooms and lights are operated by pull-cord switches.
parts.answer: Wet skin has much lower resistance so a shock current would be 100 times larger and could be fatal; a pull cord is an insulator, so wet hands never touch a switch connected to the mains.
parts.working: Wet skin current much larger / dangerous (B1); pull cord keeps wet hands away from live parts (B1)

stem: A 3.0 kW, 230 V fan heater is connected to the mains through an extension lead rated at 10 A. The lead has a total resistance of 0.15 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the heater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using this extension lead is unsafe.
parts.answer: The current (13 A) is greater than the lead's 10 A rating, so the lead will overheat.
parts.working: Compares 13 A with 10 A (B1); overheating / fire risk (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power wasted as heat in the lead.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a safer arrangement.
parts.answer: Plug the heater directly into a wall socket / use a lead rated at 13 A or more.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A simple periscope has two plane mirrors fixed parallel to each other inside a vertical tube. At what angle to the tube is each mirror fixed?
A 30°
B 45°
C 60°
D 90°
parts.working: At 45° each mirror turns the light through 90° (angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 45°), so light entering horizontally at the top leaves horizontally at the bottom. At 90° the light would be reflected straight back.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The refractive index of water is 1.33. A ray of light inside a swimming pool strikes the water surface at an angle of incidence of 50°. What happens to the ray?
A it passes into the air, bending away from the normal
B it travels along the water surface
C it is totally internally reflected
D it passes into the air without changing direction
parts.answer: C it is totally internally reflected
parts.working: Critical angle: sin c = 1/1.33, c = 48.8°. Since 50° is greater than the critical angle, the ray is totally internally reflected. A would happen only for angles below 48.8°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ray of light enters one face of a rectangular glass block at an angle and leaves through the opposite face. Describe the path of the ray.
parts.answer: It bends towards the normal on entering the glass and away from the normal on leaving; the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways.
parts.working: Towards normal entering, away from normal leaving (B1); emerges parallel to original direction (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to a ray that strikes the block along the normal.
parts.answer: It passes straight through without changing direction (it slows down).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Bilal looks into a swimming pool from the side. The pool looks shallower than it really is. Explain why.
parts.answer: Light from the bottom refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water; his eye traces the rays back in straight lines, so they seem to come from a point higher than the real bottom.
parts.working: Refraction away from normal at water–air surface (B1); rays traced back appear to come from a shallower point (B1)

stem: A ray of light passes from air into a clear liquid in a glass tank (ignore the thin glass wall). The angle of incidence in air is 55° and the angle of refraction in the liquid is 37°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the refractive index of the liquid.
parts.working: n = sin i / sin r (C1) = sin 55° / sin 37° = 1.36 (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The speed of light in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the speed of light in the liquid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the critical angle for light passing from the liquid into air.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A pair of binoculars uses right-angled glass prisms with angles of 90°, 45° and 45°. The refractive index of the glass is 1.50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the critical angle for the glass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A ray enters one of the shorter faces at right angles and strikes the longest face at an angle of incidence of 45°. Explain what happens to the ray at this face.
parts.answer: It is totally internally reflected, because 45° is greater than the critical angle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the angle through which the ray is turned by the prism.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using a prism rather than a plane mirror for this.
parts.answer: Total internal reflection reflects almost all the light / no silvered surface to tarnish / no double images.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A fish swims in a pond. The refractive index of water is 1.33.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light from a fish strikes the water surface at an angle of incidence of 30°. Calculate the angle of refraction in the air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the largest angle of incidence in the water for which light from the fish can still pass into the air.
parts.working: The critical angle: sin c = 1/1.33 (C1); c = 48.8° (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to light from the fish that strikes the surface at an angle of incidence of 60°.
parts.answer: It is totally internally reflected back into the water.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student places an object pin in front of a vertical plane mirror standing on a sheet of paper. She uses a search pin to locate the image by no-parallax and measures the object distance u and image distance v from the mirror line.
u / cm: 4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0
v / cm: 4.2, 5.9, 8.3, 9.8, 12.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (v − u) for each row and the mean of these differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the results show about the image formed by a plane mirror.
parts.answer: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (v = u within experimental error).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two sources of inaccuracy in this experiment.
parts.answer: The reflecting (silvered) surface is at the back of the glass; pins not exactly vertical; parallax when lining up pins; pin holes are wide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Use a thin mirror / line up the bases of the pins / repeat and average / use finer pins.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a longitudinal wave, in which direction do the particles of the medium vibrate?
A at right angles to the direction of energy transfer
B parallel to the direction of energy transfer
C in circles around the direction of energy transfer
D they do not vibrate; they move along with the wave
parts.answer: B parallel to the direction of energy transfer
parts.working: In a longitudinal wave (such as sound) the vibrations are parallel to the direction the wave transfers energy, forming compressions and rarefactions. A describes a transverse wave.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A wave has a period of 0.025 s and a wavelength of 1.2 m. What is the speed of the wave?
A 0.030 m/s
B 0.021 m/s
C 33 m/s
D 48 m/s
parts.answer: D 48 m/s
parts.working: f = 1/T = 1/0.025 = 40 Hz; v = fλ = 40 × 1.2 = 48 m/s. A multiplies T by λ instead of dividing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the amplitude of a wave.
parts.answer: The maximum displacement from the rest (undisturbed) position

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the wavelength.
parts.answer: The distance between a point on one wave and the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by the frequency.
parts.answer: The number of waves passing a point (or produced by the source) per second

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is meant by a wavefront.
parts.answer: A line joining points on a wave that are in step (e.g. along a crest)

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give one example of a transverse wave and one example of a longitudinal wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: light / any electromagnetic wave / water ripples; longitudinal: sound / ultrasound / seismic P-wave

stem:
A snapshot of a transverse wave on a long spring gives these values of displacement y at positions x along the spring.
x / cm: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
y / cm: 0, +3.0, 0, −3.0, 0, +3.0, 0, −3.0, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the wavelength.
parts.answer: 20 cm
parts.working: Repeat distance: crest at 5 cm to crest at 25 cm (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the amplitude.
parts.answer: 3.0 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The frequency of the wave is 5.0 Hz. Calculate the speed of the wave in m/s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the horizontal distance between a crest and the next trough.
parts.answer: 10 cm

author: HomiLabs

stem: Straight (plane) water waves in a ripple tank strike a straight barrier at an angle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the law that describes the reflection of the waves at the barrier.
parts.answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the wavelength, frequency and speed of the waves on reflection.
parts.answer: All three stay the same.
parts.working: All three unchanged (B2; two correct B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The reflected waves then pass into a region of shallower water. State and explain which of the three quantities change.
parts.answer: Speed and wavelength decrease; frequency stays the same because it is set by the source (dipper).
parts.working: Speed and wavelength decrease (B1); frequency unchanged, fixed by source (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A tsunami travels across the deep ocean at 200 m/s. It has a period of 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the tsunami in the deep ocean, in km.
parts.answer: 180 km

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the frequency of the tsunami does not change as it approaches the coast.
parts.answer: The frequency is set by the source; the same number of waves must arrive each second as left the deep water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Near the coast the speed falls to 20 m/s. Calculate the new wavelength.
parts.answer: 18 km

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the tsunami to cross 1500 km of deep ocean, in hours.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Villages in a deep valley near Murree receive long-wave radio (wavelength 1500 m) clearly but receive FM radio (wavelength 3 m) poorly. Explain why.
parts.answer: Waves diffract (spread) round obstacles; diffraction is significant when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the obstacle; the long waves (1500 m) bend around the hills into the valley but the short FM waves hardly diffract, so the hills block them.
parts.working: Diffraction round hills (B1); amount depends on wavelength compared with size of obstacle (B1); long wavelength diffracts much more than 3 m (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the wavelength and frequency of a wave when it is diffracted.
parts.answer: Both stay the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sea waves of wavelength 8 m reach a harbour wall with two entrances, one 10 m wide and one 80 m wide. State and explain which entrance lets the waves spread out more behind the wall.
parts.answer: The 10 m entrance, because its width is similar to the wavelength.
parts.working: 10 m gap (B1); gap width close to wavelength gives most diffraction (B1)

stem: A motor-driven dipper makes straight waves in a ripple tank at a frequency of 12 Hz. Using a ruler held over the water, a student measures the distance across 10 complete wavelengths as 9.6 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student measured across ten wavelengths rather than one.
parts.answer: It reduces the percentage uncertainty in the measured wavelength.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the moving waves could be made to appear stationary so they are easier to measure.
parts.answer: Use a stroboscope (flashing light) at the same frequency as the waves / take a photograph.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest one other reason why the result may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: The shadow pattern on the floor is larger than the real waves / waves move during measurement / edges of shadows are blurred.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by monochromatic light?
A light of a single frequency
B white light containing all colours
C light of a single brightness
D light that has passed through a prism
parts.answer: A light of a single frequency
parts.working: Monochromatic means one colour, i.e. a single frequency (single wavelength). White light contains a range of frequencies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An object is placed at a distance of twice the focal length (2F) from a thin converging lens. Which describes the image?
A real, inverted, same size, at 2F on the other side
B real, upright, enlarged, beyond 2F
C virtual, upright, same size, at 2F on the same side
D real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F
parts.answer: A real, inverted, same size, at 2F on the other side
parts.working: For an object at 2F, a ray diagram gives a real, inverted image of the same size at 2F on the opposite side. D is the image for an object beyond 2F.

stem: A slide projector uses a lens to form a large, sharp image of a small picture on a distant screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of lens used in the projector.
parts.answer: Converging (convex) lens

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a real image.
parts.answer: An image formed where light rays actually meet; it can be shown on a screen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two characteristics of the image on the screen.
parts.answer: Real, inverted, enlarged

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the picture on the slide must be placed upside down.
parts.answer: The lens forms an inverted image, so an upside-down slide gives an upright picture.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of visible light with the longest wavelength.
parts.answer: Red

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of visible light with the highest frequency.
parts.answer: Violet

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare the speeds of red light and violet light in a vacuum.
parts.answer: They are the same (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which of red and violet light travels more slowly in glass.
parts.answer: Violet

parts.label: e
parts.text: Name the effect that separates white light into its colours using a prism.
parts.answer: Dispersion

stem: A converging lens of focal length 5.0 cm forms a sharp image of a small illuminated object, 0.80 cm tall, on a screen. The screen is 30 cm from the lens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By drawing a scale ray diagram (or otherwise), determine the distance of the object from the lens.
parts.answer: 6.0 cm (accept 5.7–6.3 cm)
parts.working: Ray through the optical centre and ray through F from the image back to the object side, or 1/u = 1/f − 1/v (C1); u = 6.0 cm (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the height of the image on the screen.
parts.answer: 4.0 cm (accept 3.6–4.4 cm)
parts.working: Magnification = image distance ÷ object distance = 30 ÷ 6.0 = 5.0 (C1); 5.0 × 0.80 = 4.0 cm (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The screen is moved further from the lens. State the direction in which the object must be moved to give a sharp image again, and the effect on the size of the image.
parts.answer: Towards the lens (closer to the principal focus); the image becomes larger
parts.working: Object moved closer to the lens / towards F (B1); image larger (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A stamp collector uses a converging lens of focal length 5.0 cm as a magnifying glass. She holds the lens 3.0 cm from a stamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the image formed is virtual.
parts.answer: The object is closer to the lens than the principal focus, so the rays leaving the lens diverge and only appear to come from the image.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A ray diagram shows that the image is 7.5 cm from the lens. State on which side of the lens it is.
parts.answer: The same side as the object

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnification and the height of the image of a detail that is 1.2 mm tall.
parts.answer: Magnification 2.5; image height 3.0 mm
parts.working: magnification = image distance ÷ object distance = 7.5/3.0 (C1) = 2.5 (A1); 2.5 × 1.2 = 3.0 mm (A1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to a beam of light parallel to the principal axis when it passes through a diverging lens.
parts.answer: The rays spread out (diverge) and appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the incoming light.
parts.working: Rays diverge (B1); appear to come from a focus on the incident side (virtual focus) (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two characteristics of the image of a real object formed by a diverging lens.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright, diminished

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a diverging lens corrects short sight.
parts.answer: A short-sighted eye focuses light from distant objects in front of the retina; the diverging lens spreads the rays before they enter the eye; so the eye now focuses them on the retina.
parts.working: Distant object focused in front of retina (B1); diverging lens makes rays diverge more (B1); image now on the retina (B1)

stem:
A student uses an illuminated object, a converging lens and a screen. For each object distance u she moves the screen to get the sharpest image and records the image distance v.
u / cm: 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 40.0, 60.0
v / cm: 30.4, 22.8, 20.1, 17.2, 14.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use f = uv/(u + v) to calculate a value of f for each row.
parts.working: Correct method (C1); all five values to 3 s.f. (A2; −1 per error)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean value of f.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a quick method to estimate f before starting.
parts.answer: Focus a sharp image of a distant object (e.g. a window across the room) on the screen; the lens-to-screen distance is approximately f.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why it is hard to decide where the image is sharpest and suggest how to reduce this problem.
parts.answer: The image stays fairly sharp over a range of screen positions; move the screen back and forth to find the two positions where it just blurs and take the midpoint (or use a darkened room / brighter object).
parts.working: Sharp over a range (B1); valid technique (B1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A narrow beam of white light strikes the surface of a glass block at an angle of incidence of 45°. The refractive index of the glass is 1.51 for red light and 1.53 for violet light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle of refraction in the glass for red light and for violet light.
parts.answer: Red 27.9°; violet 27.5°
parts.working: sin r = sin 45° / n (C1); red: 27.9° (A1); violet: 27.5° (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which colour is deviated more and explain why white light spreads into a spectrum.
parts.answer: Violet: it has the larger refractive index (slows down more), so each colour is refracted by a different amount.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of violet light in this glass. The speed of light in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of electromagnetic wave is used by a television remote control?
A radio waves
B infrared
C ultraviolet
D X-rays
parts.answer: B infrared
parts.working: Remote controls send pulses of infrared radiation to a sensor on the TV. Radio waves are used for broadcasting, not the handset.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has frequencies just higher than those of visible light?
A infrared
B microwaves
C ultraviolet
D gamma rays
parts.answer: C ultraviolet
parts.working: In order of increasing frequency: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. Infrared lies just below visible light in frequency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum used for satellite television.
parts.answer: Microwaves

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the region used in airport baggage security scanners.
parts.answer: X-rays

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region detected by thermal imaging cameras.
parts.answer: Infrared

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the region used to sterilise surgical instruments sealed in plastic packs.
parts.answer: Gamma rays

parts.label: e
parts.text: Name the region used to check banknotes for security markings.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet

stem: At Islamabad airport a thermal imaging camera screens arriving passengers for signs of fever.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the radiation detected by the camera.
parts.answer: Infrared

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a passenger with a fever shows up more brightly.
parts.answer: A hotter body emits more infrared radiation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the speed of this radiation in a vacuum.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one other use of this type of radiation.
parts.answer: Remote controls / electric grills and toasters / short-range communication / intruder alarms / optical fibres

author: HomiLabs

stem: A mobile phone network uses signals of frequency 900 MHz and 1800 MHz. Electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the 900 MHz signal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the 1800 MHz signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum that these signals belong to.
parts.answer: Microwaves

author: HomiLabs

stem: A telecommunications company in Pakistan links its network by satellite and by optical fibre cables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why microwaves are used to communicate with satellites.
parts.answer: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere (including the ionosphere) without being reflected or strongly absorbed, and can be sent in a narrow beam.
parts.working: Pass through atmosphere / ionosphere (B1); travel in straight lines / narrow beams to the satellite (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the types of electromagnetic wave sent along optical fibres.
parts.answer: Visible light and infrared

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of optical fibres over copper cables for carrying internet data.
parts.answer: Much more data per second (higher bandwidth) / less interference / lighter / signals travel further before boosting

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two harmful effects of excessive ultraviolet radiation on people.
parts.answer: Damage to surface cells / skin cancer; eye damage (e.g. cataracts); sunburn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the exposure to ultraviolet is greater for climbers high in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan.
parts.answer: There is less atmosphere above them to absorb the ultraviolet / snow reflects it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one useful application of ultraviolet radiation.
parts.answer: Sterilising water / detecting fake banknotes / security marking

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether ultraviolet has a longer or shorter wavelength than visible light.
parts.answer: Shorter

stem: A microwave oven produces electromagnetic waves of frequency 2.45 GHz. The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the microwaves, in cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the microwaves heat the food.
parts.answer: Water molecules in the food absorb the microwave energy; their kinetic energy increases, raising the internal energy (temperature) of the food.
parts.working: Absorbed by water (in food) (B1); increases kinetic/internal energy (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the harmful effect on people of exposure to high-intensity microwaves.
parts.answer: Internal heating of body cells (tissue)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the oven has a metal case.
parts.answer: Metal reflects microwaves, keeping them inside the oven.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Five electromagnetic waves are described below. Their speed is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
P: wavelength 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
Q: frequency 1.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
R: wavelength 3.0 m
S: frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz
T: wavelength 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the missing wavelength or frequency for each wave.
parts.working: Uses v = fλ (C1); four correct (A1); all five correct (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the waves in order of increasing frequency.
parts.answer: R, Q, T, S, P

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the spectrum for each wave.
parts.answer: P X-rays (accept gamma rays); Q infrared; R radio waves; S ultraviolet; T visible light

author: HomiLabs

stem: An air-traffic radar at Karachi airport sends out short pulses of microwaves. The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pulse reflected by an aircraft returns 0.40 ms after it was sent. Calculate the distance to the aircraft in km.
parts.answer: 60 km

parts.label: b
parts.text: The radar uses waves of wavelength 3.0 cm. Calculate their frequency.
parts.answer: 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz

parts.label: c
parts.text: A pulse sent 10 s later returns after 0.38 ms. Calculate the speed at which the aircraft is approaching.
parts.working: New distance = 57 km, so 3.0 km closer (C1); 3000 ÷ 10 = 300 m/s (A1)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how sound is produced.
parts.answer: By a vibrating source / object

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a sound wave travels through air, using the terms compression and rarefaction.
parts.answer: Air particles vibrate backwards and forwards parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions (particles close together, higher pressure) and rarefactions (particles spread out, lower pressure).
parts.working: Longitudinal vibration of particles (B1); compressions = high pressure/close, rarefactions = low pressure/far apart (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: An electric bell rings inside a glass jar. Air is pumped out of the jar while the bell is still seen to be working. State what is heard and what this shows.
parts.answer: The sound becomes fainter and almost disappears; sound needs a medium (cannot travel through a vacuum).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sitar string is plucked harder. State the change in the sound and the property of the wave that changes.
parts.answer: Louder; larger amplitude

parts.label: b
parts.text: The player presses the string to make its vibrating length shorter. State the change in the sound and the property of the wave that changes.
parts.answer: Higher pitch; higher frequency

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sound is displayed on an oscilloscope. Describe how the trace changes when the sound becomes louder at the same pitch.
parts.answer: The waves become taller (larger height) with the same spacing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how the trace changes when the pitch rises at the same loudness.
parts.answer: More waves appear across the screen (closer together) with the same height.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place air, water and steel in order of increasing speed of sound.
parts.answer: Air, water, steel

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the approximate speed of sound in air.
parts.answer: About 330–350 m/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: A spectator far from the pitch sees a batter hit the ball before hearing the sound of the hit. Explain why.
parts.answer: Light travels much faster than sound (3 × 10⁸ m/s compared with about 340 m/s), so the light arrives almost at once while the sound takes a noticeable time.
parts.working: Light faster than sound (B1); sound takes measurable time over the distance (B1)

stem: Railway engineers test steel rails using ultrasound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency range of ultrasound.
parts.answer: Above 20 kHz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how ultrasound pulses can reveal a crack inside a steel rail.
parts.answer: Pulses are sent into the rail; part of the pulse is reflected by the crack, so an extra echo returns sooner than the echo from the far side of the rail.
parts.working: Pulse reflected from crack (B1); echo returns earlier than expected / extra echo (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The speed of ultrasound in steel is 5900 m/s. An echo from a crack returns 20 µs after the pulse is sent. Calculate the depth of the crack below the surface.
parts.working: Distance there and back = 5900 × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.118 m (C1); depth = 0.059 m (A1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A thunderstorm approaches a village in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boy sees a lightning flash and hears the thunder 4.5 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the lightning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the time taken by the light can be ignored.
parts.answer: Light travels about a million times faster, so its travel time is negligible (about 5 µs).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Two minutes later, the gap between flash and thunder is 3.0 s. Calculate the average speed at which the storm is approaching.
parts.answer: 4.25 m/s (about 4 m/s)
parts.working: New distance 1020 m, so storm moved 510 m (C1); 510 ÷ 120 = 4.25 m/s (A1)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bat finds insects by emitting short calls of frequency 50 kHz and listening for the echoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the bat's call in air, in mm. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s.
parts.answer: 6.8 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The echo from a moth returns 12 ms after the call. Calculate the distance to the moth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why people cannot hear the bat's call.
parts.answer: 50 kHz is above the upper limit of human hearing (20 kHz): it is ultrasound.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the range of frequencies a healthy young person can hear.
parts.answer: 20 Hz to 20 kHz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths in air of sounds at the two limits of this range. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s.
parts.answer: 17 m at 20 Hz; 0.017 m (1.7 cm) at 20 kHz

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the upper limit usually changes as a person gets older.
parts.answer: It falls (older people cannot hear the highest frequencies).

stem: A student stands 100 m from a high wall and claps at a steady rate, adjusting the rate until each clap coincides with the echo of the previous clap. A friend times 20 intervals between claps as 12.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time between one clap and the next.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of sound.
parts.working: In one interval sound travels 2 × 100 = 200 m (C1); 200 ÷ 0.60 = 333 m/s (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student timed 20 intervals rather than one.
parts.answer: Reduces the effect of reaction time / smaller percentage uncertainty in the time.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in this method.
parts.answer: Judging exactly when each clap coincides with the echo / reaction time when starting and stopping the watch / measuring 100 m accurately.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two microphones are placed 1.65 m apart in a line with a source of a sharp click. Each microphone is connected to an electronic timer, which records a time of 5.0 ms for the click to pass from the first microphone to the second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this method is more accurate than using a stopwatch over the same distance.
parts.answer: Human reaction time (about 0.2 s) is far longer than 5 ms, so a stopwatch could not measure such a short time; the electronic timer is not affected by reaction time.
parts.working: Reaction time much larger than the time measured (B1); electronic timer avoids it / measures ms precisely (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the experiment could be changed to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the time.
parts.answer: Increase the distance between the microphones (longer time).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of a 340 Hz sound in air. The speed of sound is 340 m/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ali can hear his sister talking in the next room through an open doorway, but cannot see her. Explain why.
parts.answer: Both sound and light diffract at the doorway; the amount of diffraction is large when the wavelength is similar to the width of the gap; sound wavelengths (about 1 m) are similar to a doorway so sound spreads round the corner, but light wavelengths (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m) are far smaller so light hardly spreads.
parts.working: Diffraction at the doorway (B1); depends on wavelength compared with gap (B1); sound λ ≈ door width, light λ much smaller (B1)

stem: A boy stands between two parallel cliffs in a valley and claps once. He hears the first echo 1.2 s later and the second echo 2.0 s after the clap. The speed of sound is 340 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the boy to each cliff.
parts.answer: 204 m and 340 m

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the distance between the cliffs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time at which the boy hears a third echo, from sound that has been reflected by both cliffs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?
A radon gas released from rocks and soil
B microwaves from a mobile phone mast
C infrared radiation from a room heater
D radio waves from a television transmitter
parts.answer: A radon gas released from rocks and soil
parts.working: Radon is a radioactive gas that emits ionising (alpha) radiation and is a major part of background radiation. B, C and D are electromagnetic waves that are not ionising, so they are not counted as background radiation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A household smoke detector contains a small source that emits alpha particles into an air gap between two metal plates. Why is an alpha emitter chosen?
A Alpha particles strongly ionise the air, giving a small current that falls when smoke absorbs them.
B Alpha particles pass through the plastic case and warn people nearby.
C Alpha particles are deflected by smoke into a detector, which sounds the alarm.
D Alpha particles heat the smoke so that it rises out of the detector.
parts.answer: A Alpha particles strongly ionise the air, giving a small current that falls when smoke absorbs them.
parts.working: Alpha is the most ionising radiation, so it makes many ions that carry a current across the gap; smoke particles absorb the alpha particles, the current falls and the alarm sounds. B is wrong: alpha has a very short range and is stopped by the case, which is also why the detector is safe.

stem: A factory in Lahore sterilises plastic syringes after they have been sealed in plastic packets. The packets pass close to a strong radioactive source.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which type of radiation is used and explain why it is suitable.
parts.answer: gamma radiation; it is very penetrating, so it passes through the sealed packaging to reach every part of the equipment
parts.working: B1 gamma; B1 penetrates the packaging / reaches all of the contents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the radiation sterilises the equipment.
parts.answer: the ionising radiation kills bacteria and other microorganisms (damages their cells/DNA)
parts.working: B1 kills microbes by ionisation / cell damage

parts.label: c
parts.text: A worker is worried that the syringes become radioactive. State whether she is right and give a reason.
parts.answer: no; the syringes are only exposed to (irradiated by) the radiation – they do not absorb any radioactive material, so they do not become radioactive
parts.working: B1 no, with reason: irradiation does not make the object radioactive / no radioactive nuclei are added

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sodium-24 is a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 15 hours. A sample contains 8.0 mg of sodium-24.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium-24 remaining after 60 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the fraction of the original sodium-24 nuclei that have decayed after 60 hours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the activity of the sample to fall to one quarter of its starting value.
parts.answer: 30 hours

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Polonium-210 (²¹⁰₈₄Po) decays by alpha emission to form lead (Pb). Write the decay equation.
parts.answer: ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He
parts.working: B1 alpha particle written as ⁴₂He (or ⁴₂α); B1 ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strontium-90 (⁹⁰₃₈Sr) decays by beta emission to form yttrium (Y). Write the decay equation.
parts.answer: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e
parts.working: B1 beta particle written as ⁰₋₁e (or ⁰₋₁β); B1 ⁹⁰₃₉Y

parts.label: c
parts.text: Strontium-90 has more neutrons in its nucleus than the stable isotopes of strontium. Suggest why this makes it decay by beta emission rather than by alpha emission.
parts.answer: it has an excess of neutrons; in beta decay a neutron changes into a proton (and an electron), which reduces the number of neutrons and increases the number of protons, making the nucleus more stable; strontium-90 is not a very heavy nucleus, so it does not need to lose mass by alpha emission
parts.working: B1 excess of neutrons makes it unstable; B1 beta decay turns a neutron into a proton, improving the neutron–proton balance

stem:
Engineers suspect a leak in an underground water main in Karachi. They plan to add a small amount of a radioactive tracer to the water. They can choose from four isotopes:
P: emits alpha, half-life 2 days
Q: emits gamma, half-life 6 hours
R: emits beta, half-life 30 years
S: emits gamma, half-life 5 years

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which isotope should be used. Give two reasons for your choice.
parts.answer: Q; it emits gamma, which can pass through the pipe and the ground to reach a detector at the surface; its half-life (6 hours) is long enough to complete the test but short enough that little radioactivity remains in the water supply afterwards
parts.working: B1 Q; B1 gamma passes through soil/pipe (alpha and beta would be absorbed); B1 half-life of hours: long enough for the search, short so it does not stay active in the water for long

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why isotope S is not suitable even though it is a gamma emitter.
parts.answer: its half-life is 5 years, so it would remain radioactive in the water supply for many years
parts.working: B1 long half-life → water stays contaminated for years

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the engineers use a detector to find the leak.
parts.answer: they move a detector (Geiger–Müller tube) along the ground above the pipe; the count rate is highest above the leak, where the tracer-containing water collects in the soil
parts.working: B1 move detector along route of pipe; B1 highest count rate marks the leak

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hospital stores waste containing iodine-131 (half-life 8.0 days) until its activity has fallen from 4.8 MBq to 0.30 MBq or less.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum time for which the waste must be stored.
parts.answer: 32 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: A different sample contains two isotopes, X (half-life 2.0 hours) and Y (half-life 6.0 hours). At the start each has an activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the total activity after 6.0 hours.
parts.answer: 500 Bq
parts.working: X: 3 half-lives → 800/8 = 100 Bq (M1); Y: 1 half-life → 400 Bq (M1); total 500 Bq (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the total activity of the mixed sample does not halve in equal time intervals.
parts.answer: the two isotopes decay at different rates; at first the fast-decaying X makes the total fall quickly, later almost all the activity is from Y, so the total falls more slowly (the time to halve gets longer)
parts.working: B1 different half-lives; B1 the proportion from each changes so the halving time increases with time

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cobalt-60 (⁶⁰₂₇Co), half-life 5.3 years, is used as a gamma source in some radiotherapy machines. It decays by beta emission, and the nucleus formed then emits gamma rays.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the beta decay of cobalt-60 to nickel (Ni).
parts.answer: ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + ⁰₋₁e

parts.label: b
parts.text: After the beta decay the nickel nucleus emits a gamma ray. Explain why it emits a gamma ray, and why this does not change the element.
parts.answer: the nucleus is left with excess energy (in an excited state) and loses it as a gamma ray; gamma is electromagnetic radiation with no charge and no mass, so the proton number (and nucleon number) is unchanged – it is still nickel
parts.working: B1 releases excess energy from the nucleus; B1 no change in proton number (gamma has no charge/mass)

parts.label: c
parts.text: When the source is new, a treatment needs an exposure time of 2.0 minutes. Calculate the exposure time needed to give the same dose 10.6 years later. Assume the dose received is proportional to activity × time.
parts.answer: 8.0 minutes
parts.working: 10.6 ÷ 5.3 = 2 half-lives, activity is 1/4 of its original value (C1); time × 4 = 8.0 min (A1)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures the half-life of a short-lived isotope with a Geiger–Müller tube and counter.
With no source present she records 230 counts in 10 minutes.
With the source in place she records 1544 counts in the 2 minutes starting at time 0.
She records 426 counts in the 2 minutes starting at time 45 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the background count rate in counts/min.
parts.answer: 23 counts/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected count rate due to the source at 0 min and at 45 min.
parts.answer: 749 counts/min and 190 counts/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to (b) to estimate the half-life of the isotope. Explain your method.
parts.answer: about 23 minutes (accept 22–23 min)
parts.working: 749 → 190 is a fall by a factor of about 3.9 ≈ 4, i.e. about 2 half-lives in 45 min (M1); half-life ≈ 45 ÷ 2 ≈ 23 min (A1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the background count was measured over 10 minutes and each source count over 2 minutes, rather than over a few seconds.
parts.answer: radioactive decay is random, so counts fluctuate; counting for longer gives a larger total count, so the random fluctuations are a smaller fraction and the average rate is more reliable
parts.working: B1 decay is random/counts vary; B1 longer count → more reliable average (smaller percentage variation)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What does the nucleon number of a nucleus tell you?
A the number of protons
B the number of neutrons
C the total number of protons and neutrons
D the total number of protons and electrons
parts.answer: C the total number of protons and neutrons
parts.working: Protons and neutrons are both nucleons, so the nucleon (mass) number is their total. A is the proton number; D is wrong because electrons are not in the nucleus.

stem: Three nuclides are ⁴₂He, ²⁷₁₃Al and ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of protons and the number of neutrons in each nucleus.
parts.answer: He: 2 protons, 2 neutrons; Al: 13 protons, 14 neutrons; Au: 79 protons, 118 neutrons
parts.working: B1 for each nuclide (both numbers correct)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the number of neutrons compares with the number of protons as the nuclei become heavier.
parts.answer: Light nuclei have about equal numbers; heavier nuclei have more neutrons than protons (the excess grows)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the relative charge of the gold nucleus.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student draws a table with three rows: proton, neutron, electron, and two columns: relative mass, relative charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the table by giving the relative mass and the relative charge of each particle.
parts.answer: proton: mass 1, charge +1; neutron: mass 1, charge 0; electron: mass about 1/1840 (negligible), charge −1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the atom each particle is found.
parts.answer: protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons orbit outside the nucleus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus.
parts.answer: the protons and neutrons, which are in the nucleus, each have a mass about 1840 times the mass of an electron
parts.working: B1 nucleons much more massive than electrons

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen has three isotopes. Ordinary hydrogen has no neutrons, deuterium has one neutron and tritium has two neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the nuclide notation for each of the three isotopes.
parts.answer: ¹₁H, ²₁H, ³₁H
parts.working: B1 all proton numbers 1; B1 nucleon numbers 1, 2, 3

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the three isotopes are the same and one way in which they are different.
parts.answer: same: number of protons (proton number) / same element / same number of electrons; different: number of neutrons / nucleon number / mass

parts.label: c
parts.text: Tritium is radioactive. State what this suggests about its nucleus.
parts.answer: its nucleus is unstable (it has too many neutrons for its number of protons)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each statement, write fission, fusion or both.
(i) A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei.
(ii) It is the energy source of the Sun.
(iii) It releases energy.
(iv) It is used in nuclear power stations today.
(v) Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus.
(vi) Neutrons are released that can cause the process to repeat in a chain reaction.
parts.answer: (i) fission (ii) fusion (iii) both (iv) fission (v) fusion (vi) fission
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correct; 2 marks for four or five; 1 mark for two or three

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the total mass of the products of a fission reaction compares with the total mass before the reaction.
parts.answer: it is slightly less
parts.working: B1 slightly smaller (mass is converted to energy)

stem: The diameter of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The diameter of its nucleus is about 2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the diameter of the atom is than the diameter of the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a model, the nucleus is a marble of diameter 1.0 cm placed at the centre of a cricket ground. Calculate the diameter of the atom in this model, in metres.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the model to explain why most alpha particles fired at a thin metal foil pass straight through.
parts.answer: the atom is mostly empty space; the nucleus is tiny, so most alpha particles never come close to a nucleus
parts.working: B1 mostly empty space / nucleus very small

author: HomiLabs

stem: Particles in nuclear equations are written in nuclide notation, with the nucleon number at the top left and the proton number (or charge) at the bottom left.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the nuclide notation for a proton, a neutron and an electron.
parts.answer: proton ¹₁p; neutron ¹₀n; electron ⁰₋₁e

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electron has a nucleon number of 0 in this notation.
parts.answer: its mass is negligible compared with a nucleon (and it is not a proton or neutron)
parts.working: B1 negligible mass / not a nucleon

parts.label: c
parts.text: An alpha particle is written ⁴₂He. State what particles it contains.
parts.answer: 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ⁹⁰₃₈Sr + X + 2 ¹₀n
Which nucleus is X?
A ¹⁴³₅₄Xe
B ¹⁴⁴₅₄Xe
C ¹⁴⁵₅₄Xe
D ¹⁴⁶₅₄Xe
parts.answer: B ¹⁴⁴₅₄Xe
parts.working: Nucleon numbers: 235 + 1 = 236 = 90 + A + 2, so A = 144; proton numbers: 92 = 38 + Z, so Z = 54. D (146) forgets the two neutrons released; A (143) forgets the neutron absorbed.

stem: In an alpha-particle scattering experiment, a narrow beam of alpha particles is aimed at a gold foil only a few hundred atoms thick, inside an evacuated chamber.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path of an alpha particle that (i) passes far from any nucleus, (ii) passes close to a nucleus, (iii) travels directly towards a nucleus.
parts.answer: (i) goes straight through, undeflected; (ii) is deflected (repelled) through an angle away from the nucleus; (iii) slows, stops and bounces back along its path (deflected through about 180°)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the alpha particles are deflected by the nucleus.
parts.answer: both the alpha particle and the nucleus are positively charged, so they repel

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the foil must be very thin and the apparatus kept in a vacuum.
parts.answer: thin foil: so each alpha particle interacts with (at most) one nucleus and is not absorbed; vacuum: alpha particles would be stopped by (collide with) air molecules within a few cm
parts.working: B1 thin foil reason; B1 vacuum reason

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a nuclear reactor, plutonium-239 can undergo fission:
²³⁹₉₄Pu + ¹₀n → ¹³⁴₅₄Xe + ¹⁰³₄₀Zr + 3 ¹₀n
Each fission releases about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Burning one molecule of methane (natural gas) releases about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what causes the plutonium nucleus to split.
parts.answer: It absorbs a neutron (which makes it unstable)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy is released by one fission than by burning one molecule of methane.
parts.answer: 2.3 × 10⁷ times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the total mass of the products compares with the total mass of the plutonium nucleus and neutron, and state the main form of the energy released.
parts.answer: The products have slightly less mass; the energy is released mainly as kinetic energy of the fission fragments and neutrons (which heats the reactor)
parts.working: B1 slightly less mass; B1 kinetic energy of products

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium nuclei in the Sun's core makes the products slightly less massive than the reactants. As a result the Sun loses about 4.3 × 10⁹ kg of mass every second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass the Sun loses in one day. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.7 × 10¹⁴ kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mass of the Sun is 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg. Calculate the fraction of its mass lost in one year (3.15 × 10⁷ s).
parts.answer: about 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁴

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain where this 'lost' mass goes.
parts.answer: it is converted into the energy released by fusion (radiated as light, infrared, etc.)
parts.working: B1 mass converted to energy released in fusion

author: HomiLabs

stem: The most common isotope of iron is ⁵⁶₂₆Fe. The charge on a proton is e = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the charge on the iron nucleus in terms of e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the nucleus in coulombs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mass of a proton is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Estimate the mass of the iron nucleus.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons. The nucleus is not changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For the sulfide ion ³²₁₆S²⁻, state the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
parts.answer: 16 protons, 16 neutrons, 18 electrons
parts.working: B1 protons and neutrons; B1 18 electrons (two extra)

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the iron ion ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺, state the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
parts.answer: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
parts.working: B1 protons and neutrons; B1 23 electrons (three lost)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why forming an ion does not change the element.
parts.answer: the number of protons in the nucleus (proton number) is unchanged; only electrons are gained or lost

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a sample of uranium-235, each fission releases neutrons that can cause further fissions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume every neutron released causes one new fission and each fission releases 3 neutrons. One fission happens in the first generation. Calculate the number of fissions in the 10th generation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a chain reaction.
parts.answer: neutrons released by one fission go on to cause further fissions, which release more neutrons, so the process continues by itself

parts.label: c
parts.text: In a power station only one neutron from each fission, on average, causes a further fission. State and explain what happens to the rate of fission and the power output.
parts.answer: the rate of fission stays constant, so the power output is steady (the reaction is controlled, not growing)
parts.working: B1 constant rate; B1 steady/controlled power

author: HomiLabs

stem: A nuclear power station has an electrical output of 900 MW and an overall efficiency of 33 %. Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which thermal energy must be produced in the reactor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fissions needed each second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mass of one uranium-235 nucleus is 3.9 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Calculate the mass of uranium-235 used in one day.
parts.answer: 2.9 kg

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a proposed fusion reactor, a deuterium nucleus and a tritium nucleus fuse:
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n
Each reaction releases 2.8 × 10⁻¹² J. The mass of one deuterium nucleus plus one tritium nucleus is 8.35 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of fusion reactions needed each second to supply a power of 1.0 GW.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of fuel used in one day at this power. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why fusion power stations are not yet in use, even though very little fuel is needed.
parts.answer: any two of: extremely high temperature (millions of °C) is needed so nuclei overcome repulsion; the hot plasma is very difficult to contain (no material can touch it); it is hard to get more energy out than is put in; high pressure/density is needed

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil (proton number 79) and a few are deflected through large angles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The gold foil is replaced by a foil of aluminium (proton number 13) of the same thickness. Suggest and explain how the number of large-angle deflections changes.
parts.answer: fewer large-angle deflections; the aluminium nucleus has a much smaller positive charge (13 compared with 79), so the repulsive force on the alpha particles is smaller
parts.working: B1 fewer; B1 smaller nuclear charge → weaker repulsion

parts.label: b
parts.text: The alpha particles are given more kinetic energy. Suggest and explain the effect on the deflections.
parts.answer: the deflections are smaller (fewer large-angle deflections); faster alpha particles pass each nucleus more quickly, so the same repulsive force has less time to change their direction
parts.working: B1 smaller deflections / fewer large-angle deflections; B1 reason: faster particles are turned less by the same repulsion

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says the experiment shows that the nucleus contains neutrons. Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: neutrons have no charge, so they do not repel alpha particles and cannot cause the deflections; the experiment only shows that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
parts.working: B1 neutrons uncharged → no effect on deflection; B1 shows only a small, dense, positive nucleus

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nucleus X has nucleon number 39 and contains 3 more neutrons than protons. Determine its proton number and number of neutrons.
parts.answer: 18 protons, 21 neutrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nucleus Y has the same nucleon number as X but one more proton. Write the nuclide notation for X and Y, using the symbols Ar (proton number 18) and K (proton number 19).
parts.answer: X = ³⁹₁₈Ar; Y = ³⁹₁₉K

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether X and Y are isotopes. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: no; they have different proton numbers, so they are different elements

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the ratio charge of nucleus Y ÷ charge of nucleus X.

stem: A gold nucleus ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au has a radius of about 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The mass of a nucleon is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the gold nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the nucleus, treating it as a sphere (V = 4/3 πr³).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the density of the nucleus. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³

parts.label: d
parts.text: The density of solid gold is 1.9 × 10⁴ kg/m³. Explain what the comparison tells you about the structure of a gold atom.
parts.answer: the nucleus is about 10¹³ times denser than gold, so almost all the mass is in a tiny nucleus and the rest of the atom (where the electrons are) is mostly empty space
parts.working: B1 nucleus far denser; B1 atom mostly empty space with mass concentrated in nucleus

author: HomiLabs

stem:
One fission of uranium-235 is:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ᴬ₃₈Sr + 2 ¹₀n

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the nucleon number A of the strontium nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fission fragments have too many neutrons and are radioactive. Xenon-140 decays by four beta emissions in turn. Determine the proton number and nucleon number of the nuclide formed, and name the element using: 55 caesium, 56 barium, 57 lanthanum, 58 cerium.
parts.answer: proton number 58, nucleon number 140; cerium-140
parts.working: each beta decay raises the proton number by 1 and leaves the nucleon number unchanged (M1); 54 + 4 = 58, nucleon number 140 (A1); cerium (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the waste from a fission reactor must be stored safely for a long time.
parts.answer: the fission products are radioactive, and some have long half-lives, so they remain hazardous for many years

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why both fission and fusion release energy, in terms of mass.
parts.answer: in both processes the total mass of the products is less than the total mass of the reactants; the 'missing' mass is released as energy (kinetic energy of the products)
parts.working: B1 products have less mass; B1 mass converted into energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pakistan generates part of its electricity from fission. Compare fission and fusion as ways of generating electricity, giving two advantages of fusion and one reason it is not used yet.
parts.answer: fusion advantages (any two): fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is plentiful, e.g. from water; it produces much less long-lived radioactive waste; no runaway chain reaction is possible; no carbon dioxide (shared with fission); not yet used because: very high temperatures/pressures are needed and the plasma is very hard to contain, so no reactor yet gives out more energy than it uses
parts.working: B1 each for two valid advantages of fusion; B1 valid reason it is not yet used; B1 clear comparison with fission (e.g. fission uses scarce uranium / produces long-lived waste)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a light-year?
A the time taken for light to travel from the Sun to the Earth
B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
C the speed of light measured over one year
D the time taken for the Earth to orbit the Sun
parts.answer: B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
parts.working: A light-year is a unit of distance, not time. D is one year itself; A is about 8 minutes.

stem: On a clear night far from city lights, students in the hills of northern Pakistan see a faint band of light stretching across the sky.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the faint band of light is.
parts.answer: the Milky Way – the light from billions of stars in our own galaxy, seen edge-on

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a galaxy.
parts.answer: a huge collection of billions of stars, with gas and dust, held together by gravity

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Sun looks far brighter than any other star. Explain why, even though many stars give out more light than the Sun.
parts.answer: the Sun is very much closer to the Earth than any other star

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what the Universe is made of, at the largest scale.
parts.answer: billions of galaxies (separated by mostly empty space)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A star with a mass similar to the Sun passes through several stages during its life.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each stage to its description:
Stages: protostar, main sequence (stable) star, red giant, white dwarf
Descriptions:
1 a small, hot, dense core left after the outer layers drift away
2 a cloud of gas collapsing under gravity and heating up, before fusion starts
3 a star in which fusion of hydrogen in the core balances gravity for billions of years
4 a star that has run out of hydrogen in its core and has swollen and cooled at its surface
parts.answer: protostar – 2; main sequence star – 3; red giant – 4; white dwarf – 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the cloud of gas and dust left around a white dwarf when a red giant loses its outer layers.
parts.answer: a planetary nebula

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky. It is 8.6 light-years from the Earth. One light-year is 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how long ago the light now reaching Earth from Sirius left the star.
parts.answer: 8.6 years ago

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance to Sirius in metres. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Light from the Sun takes about 8.3 minutes to reach the Earth. State which is further from Earth, the Sun or Sirius, and by roughly what factor (minutes in 8.6 years ÷ 8.3 minutes).
parts.answer: Sirius is about 5 × 10⁵ times further away

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence shows the later stages in the life of a star that is much more massive than the Sun?
A red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
C red supergiant → white dwarf → supernova
D protostar → supernova → red giant
parts.answer: B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
parts.working: Massive stars swell into red supergiants, then explode as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or (for the most massive) a black hole. A is the sequence for a star like the Sun.

stem: A particular line in the spectrum of hydrogen has a wavelength of 656 nm when measured in a laboratory. The same line in the light from galaxy A is measured as 670 nm, and from galaxy B as 700 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in wavelength of this line for each galaxy.
parts.answer: A: 14 nm; B: 44 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to this increase in wavelength.
parts.answer: redshift

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which galaxy is moving away from the Earth faster, and which galaxy is further away. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: B is moving away faster, because its light shows the larger redshift; B is further away, because the speed of recession is (approximately) proportional to distance (Hubble's law)
parts.working: B1 B faster; B1 larger change in wavelength means greater speed; B1 B further, speed ∝ distance

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Sun has been a stable star for about 4.6 billion years, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what eventually stops the Sun being a stable main sequence star.
parts.answer: the hydrogen in its core runs out (is used up by fusion)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Sun will then become a red giant.
parts.answer: the core contracts and heats up, and fusion continues around it (or of helium); the extra energy makes the outer layers expand greatly, so the surface cools and glows red
parts.working: B1 outer layers expand; B1 surface cools → red

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a star like the Sun never becomes a supernova.
parts.answer: its mass is too small; only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as supernovae

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Sun radiates energy at a rate (power) of 3.8 × 10²⁶ W.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy the Sun radiates in one day. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fusing 1 kg of hydrogen into helium releases 6.4 × 10¹⁴ J. Calculate the mass of hydrogen fused each second.
parts.answer: 5.9 × 10¹¹ kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two forces (or effects) that are balanced while the Sun is stable.
parts.answer: the inward pull of gravity and the outward pressure from the hot core (thermal/radiation pressure from fusion)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A space telescope photographs a galaxy whose light has travelled for 12 billion years. Take 1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate this distance in metres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the astronomers say they are seeing the galaxy 'as it was 12 billion years ago'.
parts.answer: the light has taken 12 billion years to reach us, so the image shows the galaxy when the light left it

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Universe is about 13.8 billion years old. State the age of the Universe when the light left the galaxy, and suggest why such observations help astronomers study how galaxies formed.
parts.answer: about 1.8 billion years; they show young galaxies from soon after the Big Bang, so astronomers can compare them with nearby (older) galaxies
parts.working: B1 1.8 billion years; B1 shows early/young galaxies

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An astronomy club analyses published data for four galaxies (1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m):
Galaxy A: distance 2.0 × 10⁸ light-years, speed of recession 4200 km/s
Galaxy B: distance 4.5 × 10⁸ light-years, speed of recession 9400 km/s
Galaxy C: distance 7.0 × 10⁸ light-years, speed of recession 11 000 km/s
Galaxy D: distance 9.0 × 10⁸ light-years, speed of recession 18 800 km/s

parts.label: a
parts.text: One of the galaxies does not fit the pattern of the others. Identify it and justify your answer.
parts.answer: galaxy C; for the others v/d is about the same, but C's speed of 11 000 km/s is much less than the expected ≈ 14 600 km/s for its distance
parts.working: B1 C; B1 comparison of v/d or expected speed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using galaxies A, B and D only, calculate a mean value for the Hubble constant H₀ in s⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: convert: d in m = d in ly × 9.5 × 10¹⁵ and v in m/s (C1); v/d = 2.21, 2.20, 2.20 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ (M1); mean 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your value of H₀ to estimate the age of the Universe in years. Take 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s.
parts.answer: 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student writes three statements about the life cycles of stars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "All stars end their lives as white dwarfs." Explain whether this is correct.
parts.answer: not correct; only stars of low/medium mass (like the Sun) become white dwarfs; much more massive stars explode as supernovae and leave a neutron star or a black hole
parts.working: B1 incorrect; B1 massive stars → supernova → neutron star/black hole

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Nothing new can be made from the remains of a supernova." Explain whether this is correct.
parts.answer: not correct; the supernova throws out a nebula of gas and dust containing heavy elements, which can collapse under gravity to form new stars and planets
parts.working: B1 incorrect; B1 nebula → new stars/planetary systems with heavier elements

parts.label: c
parts.text: "A black hole is a hole in space with no mass." Explain whether this is correct.
parts.answer: not correct; a black hole has a very large mass in a tiny volume, so its gravitational field is so strong that not even light can escape
parts.working: B1 incorrect; B1 large mass/strong gravity so light cannot escape

author: HomiLabs

stem: The cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) was released when the Universe was very young and hot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why radiation that was emitted as short-wavelength radiation is now detected as microwaves.
parts.answer: the Universe has expanded since the radiation was emitted; the expansion of space has stretched the wavelength of the radiation (an extreme redshift), so it is now in the microwave region
parts.working: B1 expansion of the Universe; B1 wavelength stretched/increased

parts.label: b
parts.text: The typical wavelength of the radiation today is about 1.06 mm. When the radiation was released, wavelengths were about 1100 times shorter. Calculate the typical wavelength when it was released, and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
parts.answer: about 9.6 × 10⁻⁷ m (960 nm); infrared (just beyond visible red light)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the CMBR is detected with almost the same intensity from every direction.
parts.answer: it was produced throughout the early Universe, which was hot and dense everywhere, so it fills all of space

author: HomiLabs

stem: A galaxy is moving away from the Earth at 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance of the galaxy from the Earth in light-years, using H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ and 1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.
parts.answer: 3.2 × 10⁸ light-years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how far the galaxy moves in one million years (1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s), in light-years.
parts.answer: 2.2 × 10⁴ light-years

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the distances of galaxies measured today are not noticeably different from those measured a century ago.
parts.answer: in a million years the galaxy moves only about 0.007 % of its distance, so the change over 100 years is far too small to detect
parts.working: B1 change is a tiny fraction of the distance

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
About how much of the total mass of the Solar System is in the Sun?
A about 50 %
B about 75 %
C about 90 %
D more than 99 %
parts.answer: D more than 99 %
parts.working: The Sun contains more than 99 % of the mass of the Solar System; even Jupiter is only about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass. This is why the Sun's gravity dominates the orbits of all the planets.

stem:
Data for five planets:
Mercury: mean distance from Sun 58 million km, mean surface temperature 167 °C
Venus: 108 million km, 464 °C
Earth: 150 million km, 15 °C
Mars: 228 million km, −65 °C
Jupiter: 778 million km, −110 °C (cloud tops)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the general pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: the further the planet is from the Sun, the lower its mean surface temperature

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the planet that does not fit the pattern.
parts.answer: Venus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a reason why this planet does not fit the pattern.
parts.answer: Venus has a very thick atmosphere (mostly carbon dioxide) that traps infrared radiation (a strong greenhouse effect)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the planets further from the Sun are colder.
parts.answer: they receive less energy from the Sun per square metre (the Sun's radiation is spread over a larger area)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Earth turns once on its axis in 24 hours. Calculate the angle the Earth turns through in one hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
parts.answer: the Earth spins on its axis from west to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole); so the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west
parts.working: B1 Earth rotates on axis; B1 direction (west to east) gives apparent east to west motion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Karachi is about 23° of longitude west of Dhaka. Calculate how many minutes later the Sun rises in Karachi than in Dhaka on the same day (assume the two cities are at the same latitude).
parts.answer: 92 minutes (about 1.5 hours)
parts.working: Earth turns 15° per hour, so 23 ÷ 15 = 1.53 h (C1) = 92 min (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the force that keeps all the planets in orbit around the Sun.
parts.answer: the Sun's gravitational force (gravity)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Neptune takes about 165 years to orbit the Sun. Give two reasons why it takes so much longer than the Earth.
parts.answer: Neptune's orbit is much larger, so it has a much longer distance to travel; the Sun's gravitational field is much weaker far from the Sun, so Neptune moves more slowly
parts.working: B1 longer orbit/distance; B1 slower speed because weaker gravitational field

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the strength of the Sun's gravitational field changes with distance from the Sun.
parts.answer: it decreases as the distance increases

stem:
The gravitational field strength g due to the Earth at different distances from the Earth's centre (R = radius of the Earth):
at R: 9.8 N/kg
at 2R: 2.45 N/kg
at 3R: 1.09 N/kg
at 4R: 0.61 N/kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how g changes with distance from the centre of the Earth.
parts.answer: g decreases as the distance increases (it falls quickly at first, then more slowly)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A satellite has a mass of 50 kg. Calculate the gravitational force on it at a distance of 2R.
parts.answer: about 120 N (122.5 N)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the mass of the satellite at a distance of 3R.
parts.answer: 50 kg

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a dwarf planet and give an example.
parts.answer: a minor planet that orbits the Sun but is smaller than the eight planets (has not cleared its orbit of other objects); e.g. Pluto (or Ceres)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where most asteroids in the Solar System are found.
parts.answer: in the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between a comet and a planet.
